There is also a growing interest in [[Vegetarian cuisine|vegetarian foods]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Maynard |first=Micheline |date=June 6, 2019 |title=The Food World's Next Big Question: What Does Generation Z Want To Eat? |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michelinemaynard/2019/06/06/the-food-worlds-next-big-question-what-does-generation-z-want-to-eat/#16b87e172684 |access-date=June 10, 2019 |work=Forbes}}</ref> For breakfast, the top food choices among Generation Z are eggs, fruits, [[Toast (food)|toast]], [[pancake]]s, and [[Breakfast cereal|cold cereals]]. As for drinks, they like milk, coffee, fruit juice, tea, and tap water. However, [[coffee]] consumption among Generation Z is lower than older cohorts.<ref name=":60">{{Cite news |last=Fernandes |first=Janice |date=February 14, 2025 |title=Gen Z's breakfast habits: How the youngest generation approaches the first meal of the day |url=https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/51614-gen-zs-breakfast-habits-how-the-youngest-generation-approaches-the-first-meal-of-the-day |access-date=November 9, 2025 |work=YouGov}}</ref> [[Milk]] consumption has declined among young people and the growing rate of [[lactose intolerance]] among the ethnically diverse Generation Z is part of the reason why.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Severson |first=Kim |date=April 4, 2023 |title=Got Milk? Not This Generation. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/04/dining/milk-dairy-industry-gen-z.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230404123304/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/04/dining/milk-dairy-industry-gen-z.html |archive-date=April 4, 2023 |access-date=April 4, 2023 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Generation Z mostly prefers to eat breakfast at home.<ref name=":60" /> [[Chick-fil-A]], which remains one of the most popular fast-food restaurant chains in the United States among teenagers, despite the owners reportedly holding "conservative" values.<ref name="The Economist-2023a" /> Other popular restaurant chains among Generation Z include [[Starbucks]], [[Chipotle Mexican Grill|Chipotle]], [[McDonald's]], and [[Olive Garden]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Vega |first=Nicholas |date=October 15, 2022 |title=Chick-fil-A is Gen Z's favorite restaurant chain in the U.S.—see what else made their top 5 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/10/15/chick-fil-a-gen-z-favorite-restaurant.html |access-date=December 9, 2025 |work=CNBC}}</ref>

==== Financial security ====
[[File:20- Comparative net worth of generations, over time.svg |thumb |Though baby boomers have accumulated more wealth than later generations, Millennials and Generation{{nbsp}}X are accumulating wealth at comparable rates to baby boomers.<ref name=VISAcompareGenerations>{{cite web |title=The great wealth transfer reality check |url=https://usa.visa.com/partner-with-us/visa-consulting-analytics/economic-insights/great-wealth-transfer-reality-check.html |publisher=VISA USA |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260711132239/https://usa.visa.com/partner-with-us/visa-consulting-analytics/economic-insights/great-wealth-transfer-reality-check.html |archive-date=July 11, 2026 |date=July 2026 |url-status=live |quote=Sources: Visa Business and Economic Insights, Federal Reserve Board, Pew Research Center and U.S. Department of Commerce}}</ref>]]
Generation Z is much more likely to turn to their parents for financial advice than Millennials.<ref name="Brown-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2019/07/16/savings-parents-say-its-embarrassing-to-rely-on-them-after-27/1705355001/|title=Gen Z, millennials: It's 'embarrassing' to rely on parents for money after 27|last=Brown|first=Dalvin|date=July 16, 2019|work=USA Today|access-date=July 23, 2019}}</ref> By 2019, credit cards became the most common form of debt for Generation Z, overtaking auto loans.<ref name="Lane-2019">{{Cite news |last=Lane |first=Ben |date=August 15, 2019 |title=Forget waiting on Millennials, Gen Z is starting to buy homes |url=https://www.housingwire.com/articles/49863-forget-waiting-on-millennials-gen-z-is-starting-to-buy-homes |access-date=August 27, 2019 |work=Housing Wire}}</ref> The financial industry expects continued growth in credit activity by Generation Z, whose rate of credit delinquency is comparable to those of the Millennials and Generation X.<ref name="Tuchscherer-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2019/08/18/credit-cards-report-gen-z-taking-more-debt/2008655001/|title=As they reach adulthood, Gen Z isn't shying away from credit cards, loans and other debt|last=Tuchscherer|first=Rebekah|date=August 18, 2019|work=USA Today|access-date=August 27, 2019}}</ref> 

While American members of Generation Z are less optimistic about the state of their national economy than Millennials,<ref>{{cite web |title=Infographic: Gen Z Voter and Political Views Election 2016 |url=http://genhq.com/igen-gen-z-stance-on-politics-infographic/ |publisher=}}</ref> they hold more positive views about their own economic prospects.<ref name="Brown-2019" /> Whereas the Millennials tend to prefer flexibility, Generation Z is more interested in certainty and stability.<ref name="Piore-2019">{{Cite web|last=Piore|first=Adam|date=June 13, 2019|title=Gen Zs are Anxious, Entrepreneurial and Determined to Avoid Their Predecessor's Mistakes|url=https://www.newsweek.com/2019/06/28/gen-zs-are-anxious-entrepreneurial-determined-avoid-their-predecessors-mistakes-1443581.html|access-date=June 26, 2019|website=Newsweek}}</ref> Whereas 23% of Millennials would leave a job if they thought they were not appreciated, only 15% of Generation Z would do the same, according to a Deloitte survey.<ref name="Boyle-2019" /> A survey from the [[World Economic Forum]] (WEF) found that three quarters of Generation Z expected to work harder than previous generations.<ref name="Desjardins-2019" /> They also strive to be financially literate.<ref name=":56">{{Cite news |last=Roepe |first=Lisa Rabasca |date=June 28, 2025 |title=Gen Z, It Turns Out, Is Great at Saving for Retirement |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/28/business/retirement/gen-z-retirement-savings.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250629170235/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/28/business/retirement/gen-z-retirement-savings.html |archive-date=June 29, 2025 |access-date=June 29, 2025 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Although some also aim to achieve financial independence and [[Early retirement|retire early]] (the FIRE lifestyle), most will have to [[Trade-off|compromise]] between owning a home and early retirement.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Conte |first=Allaire |date=April 8, 2025 |title=How Gen Z Plans To Retire by 40 Using the FIRE Movement—but Will They Own a Home? |url=https://www.realtor.com/advice/buy/gen-z-fire-movement-homeownership/ |access-date=April 30, 2025 |work=Realtor.com}}</ref> As of 2025, Gen-Z women are saving for retirement at a higher rate than men, reversing a historical trend.<ref name=":56" />

A 2025 report by the Bank of America noted that among members of Generation Z already employed, wage growth has been higher than in previous cohorts, especially among those with higher education.<ref name=":48">{{Cite news |last=Carbonaro |first=Giulia |date=March 19, 2025 |title=Gen Z To Become Richest Generation By 2035: Report |url=https://www.newsweek.com/gen-z-become-richest-generation-2035-2046355 |access-date=May 23, 2025 |work=Newsweek}}</ref> The bank also indicated that as a group, Generation Z would [[Great Wealth Transfer|inherit the enormous wealth]] accumulated by their parents and grandparents over the next decade or so.<ref name=":48" />

==== Housing and tourism ====
With regards to the housing market, they typically look for properties with amenities that are comparable to what they experienced as university students.<ref name="Pinnegar-2019">{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2019/05/14/generation-z-is-entering-rental-market-heres-how-that-will-change-things/ |title=Generation Z is entering the rental market — here's how that will change things |last=Pinnegar |first=Robert |date=May 14, 2019 |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=May 18, 2019}}</ref><ref name=":62" /> Large numbers of this cohort are already saving money for buying a home, a goal many prefer to shopping, vacationing, or having a lavish wedding,<ref name="Miller-2019c" /> or even going to college.<ref name=":55">{{Cite news |last=Delouya |first=Samantha |date=June 29, 2025 |title=Against the odds, Gen Z is breaking into the housing market |url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/06/29/economy/gen-z-young-home-buyers |access-date=June 29, 2025 |work=CNN}}</ref> They are also quite willing to have strangers as roommates in order to save on rent.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brown |first=Dalvin |date=July 26, 2019 |title=Co-living spaces: How millennials, Gen Z create affordable rent situations in big cities |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2019/07/26/gen-z-co-living-blurs-line-between-residential-and-hotel-living/1812863001/ |access-date=July 27, 2019 |work=USA Today}}</ref> By the late 2010s, the number of Zoomers who have taken out a [[mortgage]] was steadily rising.<ref name="Lane-2019" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Rasta |first=Anoushah |date=November 23, 2019 |title=Majority of Generation Z Expect to Own a Home by Age 30: Study |url=https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/national-international/Majority-of-Generation-Z-Expect-to-Own-a-Home-by-Age-30-Study-565359562.html |access-date=November 28, 2019 |work=NBC New York |department=US & World}}</ref><ref group="note">Also see the section on their [[#Transportation choices|transportation choices]].</ref> The first wave of Generation Z was buying homes at about the same rate as their grandparents, the Silent Generation, in late 2019, when they owned about 2% of the housing market.<ref name="Falcon-2020">{{Cite news |last=Falcon |first=Julia |date=January 23, 2020 |title=How much housing does Gen Z already own? |url=https://www.housingwire.com/articles/how-much-housing-does-gen-z-already-own/ |access-date=January 24, 2020 |work=Housing Wire}}</ref> Judging by the amounts of mortgages, the top housing markets for Generation Z tend to have strong local economies and low cost of living.<ref name=":62">{{Cite news |last=Trapasso |first=Claire |date=January 22, 2020 |title=Generation Z Is Buying Homes: Here's What You Need to Know About This Group |url=https://www.sfgate.com/realestate/article/Generation-Z-Is-Buying-Homes-Here-s-What-You-14994651.php |access-date=January 24, 2020 |work=SF Gate |department=Real Estate}}</ref> In general, whereas the Millennials are migrating North, Generation Z appears most interested in owning a home in the Midwest and the South.<ref name="Falcon-2020" /> The growth of remote and hybrid work after the COVID-19 pandemic has made it feasible for Generation Z to own more affordable homes farther into the suburbs.<ref name=":55" /> Indeed, Generation Z is more interested in owning suburban homes than Millennials, but are more open to options than Baby Boomers.<ref name=":47" /> As of 2025, Generation Z is outpacing the Millennials and Generation X in home ownership when they were at the same age.<ref name=":55" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Burn-Murdoch |first=John |date=January 24, 2025 |title=Gen Z Americans are leaving their European cousins in the dust |url=https://www.ft.com/content/25867e65-68ec-4af4-b110-c1232525cf5c |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250403185407/https://www.ft.com/content/25867e65-68ec-4af4-b110-c1232525cf5c |archive-date=April 3, 2025 |access-date=May 23, 2025 |work=Financial Times}}</ref> But for many, home ownership remains a distant prospect due to their low wages and high costs of living.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Burn-Murdoch |first=John |date=November 28, 2025 |title=The housing crisis is pushing Gen Z into crypto and economic nihilism |url=https://www.ft.com/content/c17ac791-548f-4dfc-b456-70d054b2ffac |archive-url=https://archive.today/20251130235144/https://www.ft.com/content/c17ac791-548f-4dfc-b456-70d054b2ffac |archive-date=November 30, 2025 |access-date=December 31, 2025 |work=Financial Times}}</ref>

As tourists, Generation Z is concerned about the impact of their travels. But affordability is a more important factor for their decision-making.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sampson |first=Sarah |date=September 10, 2019 |title=United wants Gen Z customers. Gen Z wants discounts and carbon offsets. |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/travel/2019/09/10/united-wants-gen-z-customers-gen-z-wants-discounts-carbon-offsets/ |access-date=September 14, 2019 |newspaper=The Washington Post |department=By The Way}}</ref>

=== Employment expectations and prospects ===
[[File:Job_seekers_ratio.webp|thumb|330x330px|Job seekers ratio {{legend|#0714FF|Cold job market}} {{legend|#2A9B00|Balanced job market}} {{legend|#BA3117|Hot job market}}]]
Generation Z's top career choices—becoming business people, doctors, engineers, artists, and IT workers—are not that different from generations past.<ref name="Pandey-2023">{{Cite news |last=Pandey |first=Erica |date=January 21, 2023 |title=What Gen Z wants to be when they grow up |work=Axios |url=https://www.axios.com/2023/01/21/genz-careers-boomers-millennial |access-date=January 23, 2023}}</ref> For them, the most important qualities in a job are income, fulfillment, work-life balance, and job security.<ref name="Solmon-2019b" /><ref name="Piore-2019" /><ref name="Pandey-2023" /> In particular, Generation Z prioritizes a work-life balance more than older cohorts and are highly interested in flexible work schedules.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Sy |first1=Stephanie |last2=Quran |first2=Layla |date=October 2, 2024 |title=As Gen Z overtakes boomers in the workforce, a look at the changing perspectives on jobs |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/as-gen-z-overtakes-boomers-in-the-workforce-a-look-at-the-changing-perspectives-on-jobs |access-date=October 14, 2024 |work=PBS News Hour}}</ref> Millennials and Generation Z (74%) tend to have more colleagues [[Remote work|working remotely]] for a significant portion of their time compared to the Baby Boomers (58%).<ref name="Gilchrist-2019" /> Most members of Generation Z prefer to work for a medium or large company rather than a startup or a government agency.<ref name="Desjardins-2019" /><ref name="Pandey-2023" />

Access to the Internet has made self-employment much easier than it was in the past;<ref name="Monteros-2019">{{Cite news |last=Monteros |first=Maria |date=July 24, 2019 |title=These undergraduate students are starting their own businesses to pay for college |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/these-undergraduate-students-are-starting-their-own-businesses-to-pay-for-college-2019-07-24 |access-date=July 27, 2019 |work=Market Watch}}</ref> indeed, by the mid-2010s, a majority of Generation Z were running their own businesses instead of holding "traditional" teen jobs, such as waiting tables.<ref name="Edwards-2015">{{Cite news |last=Edwards |first=Jim |date=December 5, 2015 |title=Goldman Sachs has made a chart of the generations... and it will make the millennials shudder |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/goldman-sachs-chart-of-the-generations-and-gen-z-2015-12?r=UK |access-date=June 13, 2019 |work=Business Insider}}</ref> [[Morgan Stanley]] reported in 2019 that Millennials and Generation Z have been responsible for a surge in labor participation in the United States, and that while the American workforce was expanding, other G10 countries faced a shrinking number of workers. This development alleviates concerns over America's aging population which jeopardizes the solvency of various welfare programs.<ref>{{Cite news|last=McHugh|first=Calder|date=June 11, 2019|title=Morgan Stanley: Millennials, Gen Z set to boost the US economy|work=Yahoo Finance|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/morgan-stanley-millennials-gen-z-set-to-boost-the-us-economy-160707944.html|access-date=June 15, 2019}}</ref> As of 2019, Millennials and Generation Z accounted for 38% of the American workforce, a number that is projected to rise to 58% in the incoming decade.<ref name="Gilchrist-2019">{{Cite news|last=Gilchrist|first=Karen|date=March 5, 2019|title=How millennials and Gen Z are reshaping the future of the workforce|work=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2019/03/05/how-millennials-and-gen-z-are-reshaping-the-future-of-the-workforce.html|access-date=July 11, 2019}}</ref>

Due to declining interest in higher education and a tight labor market, in the early 2020s, young Americans could expect to be hired right after graduating high school.<ref name="Moody-2022">{{Cite news |last=Moody |first=Josh |date=May 26, 2022 |title=A 5th Straight Semester of Enrollment Declines |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2022/05/26/nsc-report-shows-total-enrollment-down-41-percent |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220817192456/https://www.insidehighered.com/views/2022/08/16/higher-ed-must-change-or-die-opinion |archive-date=August 17, 2022 |access-date=August 21, 2022 |work=Inside Higher Education}}</ref> In May 2023, the unemployment rate of Americans aged 16 to 24 was 7.5%, the lowest in 70 years.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Napolitano |first=Elizabeth |date=May 17, 2023 |title=The class of 2023 is entering the strongest job market in 70 years |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/youth-unemployment-70-year-low-epi-class-of-2023/ |access-date=July 21, 2023 |work=CBS News}}</ref> Among teenagers 16 to 19, employment numbers have gone up, though not to the level seen among the Baby Boomers and Generation X when they were teenagers due to a variety of factors, including jobs being automated, outsourced, or given to immigrants, and state governments regulating the job market more tightly.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nawaz |first=Amna |date=June 7, 2024 |title=After a decades-long decline in teen employment, Gen Z is reversing the trend |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/after-a-decades-long-decline-in-teen-employment-gen-z-is-reversing-the-trend |access-date=June 8, 2024 |work=PBS Newshour}}</ref> Yet despite a relatively strong labor market and falling inflation, young Americans tend to be pessimistic about their economic prospects, worrying about a possible recession, expensive housing, and the possibility of being laid off.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pazzanese |first=Christina |date=July 19, 2023 |title=The economy keeps getting better. Our moods? Not so much. |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2023/07/the-economy-keeps-getting-better-our-moods-not-so-much/ |access-date=July 21, 2023 |work=The Harvard Gazette |department=Business}}</ref>

Anxious about student debt, industrial automation, and artificial intelligence, Generation Z is increasingly interested in skilled trades, which they and their parents view as quicker and more affordable paths towards prosperity.<ref name=":23">{{Cite news |last=Royle |first=Orianna Rosa |date=April 4, 2024 |title=More Gen Z are choosing trade schools over college to become welders and carpenters because 'it's a straight path to a six-figure job' |url=https://fortune.com/2024/04/04/gen-z-choosing-trade-schools-college-welders-carpenters-six-figure-job/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240404112904/https://fortune.com/2024/04/04/gen-z-choosing-trade-schools-college-welders-carpenters-six-figure-job/ |archive-date=April 4, 2024 |access-date=October 13, 2024 |work=Fortune}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Cerullo |first1=Megan |last2=Sherter |first2=Alain |date=October 1, 2025 |title=As AI threatens white-collar work, more young Americans choose blue-collar careers |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ai-artificial-intelligence-work-trade-jobs/ |access-date=October 4, 2025 |work=CBS News}}</ref>  Generation Z is more concerned about mass unemployment due to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than [[outsourcing]] or immigration.<ref name=":63">{{Cite news |last=Peck |first=Emily |date=December 4, 2025 |title=Gen Z loses faith in America |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/12/04/gen-z-ai-economic-anxiety-harvard-poll |access-date=December 26, 2025 |work=Axios}}</ref> Indeed, many entry-level white-collar positions have been eliminated by AI,<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 18, 2025 |title=Ditch textbooks and learn how to use a wrench to AI-proof your job? |url=https://www.economist.com/international/2025/12/18/ditch-textbooks-and-learn-how-to-use-a-wrench-to-ai-proof-your-job |archive-url=https://archive.today/20251218135752/https://www.economist.com/international/2025/12/18/ditch-textbooks-and-learn-how-to-use-a-wrench-to-ai-proof-your-job |archive-date=December 18, 2025 |access-date=February 5, 2026 |work=The Economist}}</ref> and since the late 2010s, the United States faces a shortage of [[Blue-collar worker|blue-collar workers]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mindlin |first=Alan |date=October 30, 2019 |title=Gen Z Is the Answer to the Skills Gap— They Just Don't Know It Yet |url=https://www.industryweek.com/talent/gen-z-answer-skills-gap-they-just-don-t-know-it-yet |access-date=November 3, 2019 |work=Industry Week |department=Talent}}</ref> Whenever they find themselves short on skills, Generation Z will pick up what they need using the Internet.<ref name="Solmon-2019b" /> Millennials and Generation Z are overwhelmingly more likely than Baby Boomers to think that it is the job of employees to train themselves.<ref name="Gilchrist-2019" />

=== Transportation choices ===
Many members of  Generation Z no longer view car ownership as a [[status symbol]], a life milestone, or a ticket to freedom.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Osaka |first=Shannon |date=February 13, 2023 |title='I'll call an Uber or 911': Why Gen Z doesn't want to drive |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-solutions/2023/02/13/gen-z-driving-less-uber/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230216062549/https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-solutions/2023/02/13/gen-z-driving-less-uber/ |archive-date=February 16, 2023 |access-date=March 27, 2023 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> However, large swaths of this cohort have not had a driver's license or owned a car because of their economic situation rather than their concerns for the environment or [[Car-free movement|dislike of cars]]. Moreover, decades of [[Car dependency|auto-centric]] urban development in the United States have led to under-investment in walkable neighborhoods, [[Bike lane|bicycle lanes]], and [[Public transportation in the United States|public transit]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Zipper |first=David |date=March 1, 2023 |title=Gen Z's Turn Against Driving Is a Mirage |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-03-01/is-gen-z-really-done-with-driving-cars-don-t-bet-on-it |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230301193442/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-03-01/is-gen-z-really-done-with-driving-cars-don-t-bet-on-it |archive-date=March 1, 2023 |access-date=June 10, 2025 |work=Bloomberg}}</ref> The number of Generation Z consumers taking out auto loans was rising drastically during the late 2010s.<ref name="Lane-2019" /> While a significant portion of Generation Z consider environmental friendliness to be an important factor, more than their predecessors when they were at the same age, affordability was much for important to them. Generation Z is not particularly concerned with style or brand; they are more interested in safety. They tend to be more receptive towards self-driving cars.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gardner |first=Greg |date=March 16, 2016 |title=Generation Z prefers cheap green cars, study finds |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/autos/sc-generation-z-autos-0324-20160316-story.html |access-date=June 7, 2019 |work=Detroit Free Press (via the Chicago Tribune)}}</ref> They are also interested in the interior electronic technology of the cars they might purchase. More specifically, they would like to be able to hook up their smartphones to the [[Bluetooth]]-capable audio systems and backup cameras.<ref>{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=June 17, 2019 |title=Decoding Gen Z the car buyer |url=https://www.autonews.com/sponsored/decoding-gen-z-car-buyer |access-date=June 24, 2019 |work=Automotive News}}</ref>

== Education ==
{{See also|Education in the United States}}Generation Z is more likely to search for the information they need on the Internet rather than going through a book and are accustomed to learning by watching videos.<ref name="Mirabella-2019" /> A survey by the Pew Research Center found that teenage girls were more likely to feel excited about what they learned at school than boys.<ref name="Livingston-2019" /> A 2022 poll by YPulse found that the top five sets of skills Millennials and Generation Z wished they had learned at school were managing mental health, self-defense, survival skills and basic first aid, cooking, and personal finance.<ref>{{Cite web|date=January 18, 2022|title=The Skills Gen Z & Millennials Wish They Learned In School|url=https://www.ypulse.com/article/2022/01/18/the-skills-gen-z-millennials-wish-they-learned-in-school/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220119004945/https://www.ypulse.com/article/2022/01/18/the-skills-gen-z-millennials-wish-they-learned-in-school/|archive-date=January 19, 2022|access-date=January 25, 2022|website=YPulse}}</ref>

During the 2010s, the reading proficiency and mathematical literacy American schoolchildren as a group were on a decline,<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Goldstein |first=Dana |date=December 3, 2019 |title='It Just Isn't Working': Test Scores Cast Doubt on U.S. Education Efforts |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/03/us/us-students-international-test-scores.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20191203152714/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/03/us/us-students-international-test-scores.html |archive-date=December 3, 2019 |access-date=May 6, 2023 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> putting them behind their peers in many other nations, especially in East Asia.<ref name="Wai-2015">{{Cite news |last1=Wai |first1=Jonathan |last2=Makel |first2=Matthew C. |date=September 4, 2015 |title=How do academic prodigies spend their time and why does that matter? |url=https://theconversation.com/how-do-academic-prodigies-spend-their-time-and-why-does-that-matter-46594 |access-date=December 19, 2020 |work=The Conversation}}</ref><ref name="DeSilver-2017">{{Cite news |last=DeSilver |first=Drew |date=February 15, 2017 |title=U.S. students' academic achievement still lags that of their peers in many other countries |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2017/02/15/u-s-students-internationally-math-science/ |access-date=November 21, 2020 |work=Pew Research Center}}</ref> Many American public schools suffer from inadequate or dated facilities. Some schools even leak when it rains. In its 2017 report on American infrastructure, the [[American Society of Civil Engineers]] (ASCE) gave public schools a score of D+.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 21, 2019 |title=America's infrastructure is crumbling and these people are suffering because of it |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/06/17/us/crumbling-american-infrastructure/index.html |access-date=June 23, 2019 |website=CNN}}</ref> On the other hand, the majority of American public schools have acquired access to broadband Internet service, thereby increasing the frequency of digital learning.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mathewson |first=Tara Garcia |date=October 23, 2019 |title=Nearly all American classrooms can now connect to high-speed internet, effectively closing the "connectivity divide" |url=https://hechingerreport.org/nearly-all-american-classrooms-can-now-connect-to-high-speed-internet-effectively-closing-the-connectivity-divide/ |access-date=November 10, 2019 |work=Hechinger Report |department=Future of Learning}}</ref>

The COVID-19 pandemic has badly disrupted the American education system.<ref name="Hubler-2022">{{Cite news |last=Hubler |first=Shawn |date=May 17, 2022 |title=With Plunging Enrollment, a 'Seismic Hit' to Public Schools |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/17/us/public-schools-falling-enrollment.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220518185345/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/17/us/public-schools-falling-enrollment.html |archive-date=May 18, 2022 |access-date=September 1, 2022 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> In the early 2020s, different school districts report significant shortages of teachers.<ref name="Martin-2022">{{Cite news |last=Martin |first=Martin |date=August 21, 2022 |title=Teachers share why they left their job during the pandemic |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/08/21/1118702042/teachers-share-why-they-left-their-job-during-the-pandemic |access-date=August 23, 2022 |work=National Public Radio}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Natanson |first=Hannah |date=August 3, 2022 |title='Never seen it this bad': America faces catastrophic teacher shortage |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2022/08/03/school-teacher-shortage/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220803134907/https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2022/08/03/school-teacher-shortage/ |archive-date=August 3, 2022 |access-date=August 23, 2022 |newspaper=The Washington Post |department=Education}}</ref> This problem is not new but it mostly affects students in economically deprived areas.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 21, 2022 |title=America's new "national teacher shortage" is neither new nor national |url=https://www.economist.com/united-states/2022/08/21/americas-new-national-teacher-shortage-is-neither-new-nor-national |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220821205559/https://www.economist.com/united-states/2022/08/21/americas-new-national-teacher-shortage-is-neither-new-nor-national |archive-date=August 21, 2022 |access-date=August 23, 2022 |newspaper=The Economist}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Fortin |first1=Jacey |last2=Fawcett |first2=Eliza |date=August 29, 2022 |title=How Bad Is the Teacher Shortage? Depends Where You Live. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/29/us/schools-teacher-shortages.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220901160033/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/29/us/schools-teacher-shortages.html?action=click&module=RelatedLinks&pgtype=Article |archive-date=September 1, 2022 |access-date=September 1, 2022 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Public schools across the United States have had falling enrollments due to population decline and defections to private schools and [[Homeschooling in the United States|home schooling]]. As a result, their funding has also fallen.<ref name="Hubler-2022" />

Political activists are demanding that books dealing with sensitive topics relating to race and sexuality and those that include coarse language and explicit violence be [[Book censorship in the United States|removed]] from [[School library|school libraries]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Zurcher |first=Anthony |date=February 7, 2022 |title=Why are certain school books being banned in US? |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-60261660 |work=BBC News |department=US & Canada}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Harris |first1=Elizabeth A. |last2=Alexandra |first2=Alter |date=February 8, 2022 |title=Book Ban Efforts Spread Across the U.S. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/31/briefing/book-banning-debate.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220330142621/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/01/30/books/book-ban-us-schools.html |archive-date=March 30, 2022 |access-date=August 23, 2022 |work=The New York Times |department=Books}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Mazariegos |first1=Miranda |last2=Collins Sullivan |first2=Meghan |date=April 4, 2022 |title=Efforts to ban books jumped an 'unprecedented' four-fold in 2021, ALA report says |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/04/04/1090067026/efforts-to-ban-books-jumped-an-unprecedented-four-fold-in-2021-ala-report-says |access-date=August 23, 2022 |work=National Public Radio |department=Book News & Features}}</ref> How to educate students on American history has been a source of fierce debates,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Urist |first=Jacoba |date=February 24, 2024 |title=Who Should Decide How Students Learn About America's Past? |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/education/archive/2015/02/who-should-decide-how-students-learn-about-americas-past/385928/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220928220821/https://www.theatlantic.com/education/archive/2015/02/who-should-decide-how-students-learn-about-americas-past/385928/ |archive-date=September 28, 2022 |access-date=October 25, 2024 |work=The Atlantic}}</ref> as has the teaching of race and sexuality.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Price |first=Michelle L. |date=February 11, 2023 |title=Schools become flashpoint for Republicans eyeing White House |url=https://apnews.com/article/ron-desantis-politics-united-states-government-2022-midterm-elections-donald-trump-c65049b0c64206996dd1bea4cee65b81 |access-date=February 11, 2023 |work=Associated Press}}</ref> Support for parents' rights in deciding their children's educational contents and [[school choice]], or the redirecting of tax money via [[School voucher|vouchers]] to fund private schools, has grown considerably.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Stanford |first=Libby |date=February 22, 2023 |title=What the Push for Parents' Rights Means for Schools |url=https://www.edweek.org/leadership/what-the-push-for-parents-rights-means-for-schools/2023/02 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230225163923/https://www.edweek.org/leadership/what-the-push-for-parents-rights-means-for-schools/2023/02 |archive-date=February 25, 2023 |access-date=February 25, 2023 |work=Education Week}}</ref> To pacify angry parents and to comply with new state laws, many schoolteachers have opted to remove certain items from their lessons.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Natanson |first=Hannah |date=March 6, 2023 |title='Slavery was wrong' and 5 other things some educators won't teach anymore |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2023/03/06/slavery-was-wrong-5-other-things-educators-wont-teach-anymore/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230316141049/https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2023/03/06/slavery-was-wrong-5-other-things-educators-wont-teach-anymore/ |archive-date=March 16, 2023 |access-date=April 17, 2023 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref>

=== K-12 ===
[[File:D'Nealian Cursive.svg|thumb|D'Nealian cursive script]]
Since the 2000s, cursive writing has been de-emphasized in public education.<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> As a result, Generation Z are less likely to read and write in cursive.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Faust |first1=Drew Gilpin |author-link=Drew Gilpin Faust |date=16 September 2022 |title=Gen Z Never Learned to Read Cursive |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2022/10/gen-z-handwriting-teaching-cursive-history/671246/ |work=[[The Atlantic]] |language=en}}</ref> Some states introduced legislation to teach it in their jurisdiction,<ref name="Rueb-2019">{{Cite news |last=Rueb |first=Emily |date=April 13, 2019 |title=Cursive Seemed to Go the Way of Quills and Parchment. Now It's Coming Back |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/13/education/cursive-writing.html?fal |access-date=May 15, 2019 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> partly because some 80% of historical records and documents of the United States was written by hand in cursive.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bruno |first=Debra |date=June 17, 2019 |title=The National Archives has billions of handwritten documents. With cursive skills declining, how will we read them? |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/magazine/the-national-archives-has-billions-of-handwritten-documents-with-cursive-skills-declining-how-will-we-read-them/2019/06/14/cbc44028-5c92-11e9-9625-01d48d50ef75_story.html |access-date=August 10, 2019 |newspaper=The Washington Post |department=Magazine}}</ref>

The percentage of American fourth-graders proficient in reading declined during the late 2010s, according to the [[National Assessment of Educational Progress]] (NAEP).<ref name="Green-2019">{{Cite news |last1=Green |first1=Erica L. |last2=Goldstein |first2=Dana |date=October 30, 2019 |title=Reading Scores on National Exam Decline in Half the States |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/30/us/reading-scores-national-exam.html |access-date=May 6, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20191031033020/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/30/us/reading-scores-national-exam.html |archive-date=October 31, 2019}}</ref> There have been numerous reports in the 2010s on how U.S. students were falling behind their international counterparts in the STEM subjects, especially those from (East) Asia.<ref name="Wai-2015" /> For example, American schoolchildren put up a mediocre performance on the  [[Programme for International Student Assessment|Program for International Student Assessment]] (PISA), administered to fifteen-year-old students around the world on reading comprehension, mathematics, and science, falling in the middle of the pack in 2015.<ref name="DeSilver-2017" /> In fact, reading scores dropped for all ethnic groups except Asians in the late 2010s, according to the NAEP.<ref name="Green-2019" /> Nevertheless, American students ranked above the OECD average in science and [[computer literacy]], as of 2021.<ref name="Rotermund-2021">{{Cite web |last1=Rotermund |first1=Susan |last2=Burke |first2=Amy |date=July 8, 2021 |title=Elementary and Secondary STEM Education - Executive Summary |url=https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsb20211/executive-summary |access-date=January 27, 2023 |website=National Science Foundation}}</ref> As of 2024, NAEP data showed that the reading and mathematical skills of American schoolchildren on average still had not recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, while the strongest students had regained lost grounds, the weakest continued to fall behind.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Binkley |first=Collin |date=January 25, 2025 |title=US children fall further behind in reading, make little improvement in math on national exam |url=https://apnews.com/article/naep-test-scores-nations-report-card-school-60150156e41b8518be3b6eabf77d0c66 |access-date=May 26, 2025 |work=Associated Press}}</ref> An emphasis on rote memorization and speed gives as many as one in three students age five and up [[mathematical anxiety]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Boaler |first1=Jo |author-link=Jo Boaler |last2=Zoido |first2=Pablo |date=November 1, 2016 |title=Why Math Education in the U.S. Doesn't Add Up |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-math-education-in-the-u-s-doesn-t-add-up/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220823231901/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-math-education-in-the-u-s-doesn-t-add-up/ |archive-date=August 23, 2022 |access-date=August 23, 2022 |work=[[Scientific American Mind]]}}</ref> Meanwhile, an increasing number of parents opted to send their children to enrichment and accelerated learning after-school or summer programs in the subject. By the mid-2010s, however, some public schools have begun offering enrichment programs to their students.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tyre |first=Peg |date=February 8, 2016 |title=The Math Revolution |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2016/03/the-math-revolution/426855/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200628224704/https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2016/03/the-math-revolution/426855/ |archive-date=June 28, 2020 |access-date=February 4, 2021 |work=The Atlantic}}</ref>
[[File:PISA Science Scores (2022).png|center]]
Although passing a high school physics course is linked to graduating from college with a [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] degree,<ref name="Mathewson-2018">{{Cite news|url=https://hechingerreport.org/one-reason-students-arent-prepared-for-stem-careers-no-physics-in-high-school/?icid=related|title=One reason students aren't prepared for STEM careers? No physics in high school|last=Mathewson|first=Tara Garcia|date=March 9, 2018|work=The Hechinger Report|access-date=October 26, 2019|department=Future of Learning}}</ref> something that is increasingly popular among Generation Z,<ref name="Solman-2019" /> just under two-fifths of high school graduates did in 2013, according to the [[American Institute of Physics]].<ref name="Mathewson-2018" />

[[Sex education in the United States|Sex education]] has been reformed. While traditional lessons involving bananas and condoms remain common, newer approaches that emphasize financial responsibility and character development have been implemented. These reforms play a role in the significant drop in [[Teenage pregnancy in the United States|teenage birthrates]].<ref name="Cha-2016">{{Cite news|last=Cha|first=Ariana|date=April 28, 2016|title=Teen birthrate hits all-time low, led by 50 percent decline among Hispanics and blacks|newspaper=The Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/to-your-health/wp/2016/04/28/teen-birth-rate-hits-all-time-low-led-by-50-percent-decline-among-hispanics-and-blacks/|access-date=May 15, 2019}}</ref><ref group="note">Also see the section on their [[#Early sexual intercourse and adolescent pregnancy|sexual and reproductive habits]].</ref>

By the mid-2010s, over four-fifths of American high school students graduate on time and over 70% enroll in college right after graduation. However, nationally, only one-quarter of American high school seniors are able to do grade-level math and only 37% are proficient in reading,<ref name="Gonser-2018" /> yet about half graduate from high school as A students, prompting concerns of [[grade inflation]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wang |first=Amy X. |date=July 19, 2017 |title=No wonder young Americans feel so important, when half of them finish high school as A students |work=Quartz |url=https://qz.com/1032183/no-wonder-young-americans-feel-so-important-when-half-of-them-finish-high-school-as-a-students/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20210619224958/https://qz.com/1032183/no-wonder-young-americans-feel-so-important-when-half-of-them-finish-high-school-as-a-students/ |archive-date=June 19, 2021}}</ref> In addition, while 93% of middle school students said they want to attend college, only 26% go on to do so and graduate within six years. Critics argue that American high schools are not giving students they need for their future lives and careers. On top of the high costs of collegiate education, the vacancy of potentially millions of skilled jobs that do not require a university degree is making lawmakers reconsider their stance on tertiary education.<ref name="Gonser-2018">{{Cite news|last=Gonser|first=Sarah|date=April 12, 2018|title=Students are being prepared for jobs that no longer exist. Here's how that could change.|work=NBC News|department=Culture Matters|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/students-are-being-prepared-jobs-no-longer-exist-here-s-n865096|access-date=October 25, 2019}}</ref>
[[File:SAT Takers by Year.png|center|thumb|605x605px|Except during the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of students taking the SAT has grown. But as more and more students take the SAT, average scores continue to decline.<ref name="Twenge-2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Twenge |first1=Jean |last2=Campbell |first2=W. Keith |last3=Sherman |first3=Ryne A. |date=2019 |title=Declines in vocabulary among American adults within levels of educational attainment, 1974–2016 |journal=Intelligence |volume=76 |article-number=101377 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2019.101377 |s2cid=200037032 }}</ref>]]
Students' scores have been falling on a variety of standardized tests, such as the [[SAT]], and in all subjects, especially in mathematics,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Binkey |first=Collin |date=October 24, 2022 |title=Test scores show how COVID set kids back across the U.S. |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/test-scores-show-how-covid-set-kids-back-across-the-u-s |access-date=December 31, 2022 |work=PBS Newshour}}</ref> a trend found among students of all backgrounds.<ref name="Sparks-2022">{{Cite news |last=Sparks |first=Sarah D. |date=October 24, 2022 |title=Explaining That Steep Drop in Math Scores on NAEP: 5 Takeaways |url=https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/explaining-that-steep-drop-in-math-scores-on-naep-5-takeaways/2022/10 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230320173042/https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/explaining-that-steep-drop-in-math-scores-on-naep-5-takeaways/2022/10 |archive-date=March 20, 2023 |access-date=April 25, 2023 |work=Education Week}}</ref><ref name="Chapman-2022">{{Cite news |last=Chapman |first=Ben |date=October 24, 2022 |title=Math Scores Dropped in Every State During Pandemic, Report Card Shows |url=https://www.wsj.com/amp/articles/math-scores-dropped-in-every-state-during-pandemic-report-card-shows-11666584062 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20221024123306/https://www.wsj.com/amp/articles/math-scores-dropped-in-every-state-during-pandemic-report-card-shows-11666584062 |archive-date=October 24, 2022 |access-date=May 18, 2023 |work=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> After the COVID-19 pandemic, the entire cohort of college students in the 2022–23 academic year have lower average grades and mathematical standards.<ref name="Fawcett-2022">{{Cite news |last=Fawcett |first=Eliza |date=November 1, 2022 |title=The Pandemic Generation Goes to College. It Has Not Been Easy. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/01/us/covid-college-students.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20221101154830/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/01/us/covid-college-students.html |archive-date=November 1, 2022 |access-date=May 25, 2023 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

=== Post-secondary ===
==== Technical, trades, and vocational schools ====
During the 2010s, the value higher education came under heightened skepticism due to rising costs and disappointing results.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Marcus |first=Jon |date=January 22, 2016 |title=Facing skepticism, colleges set out to prove their value |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/facing-skepticism-colleges-set-out-to-prove-their-value |access-date=October 2, 2019 |work=PBS Newshour}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Paterson |first=James |date=July 3, 2018 |title=Yet another report says fewer Americans value 4-year degree |url=https://www.educationdive.com/news/yet-another-report-says-fewer-americans-value-4-year-degree/526820/ |access-date=August 2, 2019 |work=Education Dive}}</ref> According to the [[United States Department of Education|Department of Education]], people with technical or vocational training are slightly more likely to be employed than those with a bachelor's degree and significantly more likely to be employed in their fields of specialty.<ref name="Krupnick-2017">{{Cite news |last=Krupnick |first=Matt |date=August 29, 2017 |title=After decades of pushing bachelor's degrees, U.S. needs more tradespeople |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/decades-pushing-bachelors-degrees-u-s-needs-tradespeople |access-date=May 17, 2019 |work=PBS Newshour}}</ref> By the late 2010s, the United States was facing a shortage of skilled tradespeople,<ref name="Krupnick-2017" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Frazee |first=Gretchen |date=November 16, 2018 |title=Manufacturers say their worker shortage is getting worse. Here's why |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/making-sense/manufacturers-say-their-job-shortage-is-getting-worse-heres-why |access-date=May 17, 2019 |work=PBS Newshour}}</ref> because a majority of high-school students were still aiming for colleges and universities.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Gross |first1=Ashley |last2=Marcus |first2=Jon |date=April 25, 2018 |title=High-Paying Trade Jobs Sit Empty, While High School Grads Line Up For University |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/ed/2018/04/25/605092520/high-paying-trade-jobs-sit-empty-while-high-school-grads-line-up-for-university |access-date=October 14, 2024 |work=National Public Radio}}</ref> But things were changing as more and more members of Generation Z considered alternatives to higher education.<ref name="Industry Week-2019" /> [[Career counseling|Career counselors]] are in extremely high demand; they are not only called for not just appointments invited to career fairs and orientation sessions for new students.<ref name="Piore-2019" /> With growing numbers of high-school students opting for trade schools and vocational training programs,<ref name=":23" /> enrollments in higher education have been falling.<ref name="Nadworny-2018" /><ref name="Moody-2022" />

==== Colleges and universities ====
{{See also|Higher education in the United States|Higher education bubble in the United States|Elite overproduction}}[[File:US Student Loans (FRED).png|thumb|400x400px|Unlike their predecessors, Generation Z aims to avoid accumulating so much student debt.<ref name="Solman-2019" />]]Due to low standards and requirements in high school, many Americans are entering institutions of higher learning, including elite schools, with deficient reading comprehension skills and are unable and unwilling to complete long reading assignments.<ref name=":30">{{Cite news |last=McMurtrie |first=Beth |date=May 9, 2024 |title=Is This the End of Reading? |url=https://www.chronicle.com/article/is-this-the-end-of-reading |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240515205236/https://www.chronicle.com/article/is-this-the-end-of-reading |archive-date=May 15, 2024 |access-date=October 15, 2024 |work=The Chronicle of Higher Education}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Horowitch |first=Rose |date=October 1, 2024 |title=The Elite College Students Who Can't Read Books |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2024/11/the-elite-college-students-who-cant-read-books/679945/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241001114053/https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2024/11/the-elite-college-students-who-cant-read-books/679945/ |archive-date=October 1, 2024 |access-date=October 15, 2024 |work=The Atlantic}}</ref> In addition, about a quarter of American university students failed to graduate within six years in the late 2010s and those who did faced [[Diminishing returns|diminishing wage premiums]].<ref name="The Economist-2020a">{{Cite news |date=August 8, 2020 |title=Covid-19 will be painful for universities, but also bring change |url=https://www.economist.com/leaders/2020/08/08/covid-19-will-be-painful-for-universities-but-also-bring-change |access-date=December 3, 2020 |newspaper=The Economist}}</ref>

As Generation Z enters high school and preparing for college, a primary concern is paying for a higher education without acquiring debt.<ref name="Hawkins">{{cite web |last=Hawkins |first=B. Denise |title=Here Comes Generation Z. What Makes Them Tick? |url=http://neatoday.org/2015/07/13/here-comes-generation-z-what-makes-them-tick/ |access-date=10 December 2015 |website=NEA Today}}</ref> As of 2019, the total college debt has exceeded $1.5 trillion, and two out of three college graduates are saddled with debt.<ref name="Solman-2019" /> In response to these challenges, many schools have diversified their sources of revenue in order to offer their students greater tuition discounts.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Paterson |first=James |date=May 10, 2019 |title=Tuition discounts reach record high (again) as colleges diversify revenue |url=https://www.educationdive.com/news/tuition-discounts-reach-record-high-again-as-colleges-diversify-revenue/554523/ |access-date=November 28, 2019 |work=Education Dive |department=Brief}}</ref> Students also report interest in [[Reserve Officers' Training Corps]] (ROTC) programs as a means of covering college costs.<ref name="Hawkins" /> Indeed, college subsidies are one of the most attractive things about signing up for military service. Another enticement is signing bonuses, whose amounts vary according to specialty.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Fadel |first1=Leila |last2=Morris |first2=Amanda |date=January 6, 2019 |title=After Falling Short, U.S. Army Gets Creative With New Recruiting Strategy |url=https://www.npr.org/2019/01/06/682608011/after-falling-short-u-s-army-gets-creative-with-new-recruiting-strategy |access-date=July 11, 2019 |work=NPR}}</ref>

Domestic undergraduate enrollment since the early 2010s.<ref name="Nadworny-2018">{{Cite news|last=Nadworny|first=Elissa|date=May 25, 2018|title=Why Is Undergraduate College Enrollment Declining?|work=NPR|department=Education|url=https://www.npr.org/2018/05/25/614315950/why-is-undergraduate-college-enrollment-declining|access-date=November 28, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Marcus |first=Jon |date=May 22, 2021 |title=Declining birthrate means hard times ahead for colleges |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/education/college-enrollment-birthrate-decline/2021/05/21/52d7e5a6-ba47-11eb-a5fe-bb49dc89a248_story.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20210522173449/https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/education/college-enrollment-birthrate-decline/2021/05/21/52d7e5a6-ba47-11eb-a5fe-bb49dc89a248_story.html |archive-date=May 22, 2021 |access-date=November 22, 2024 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref> Due to population aging, the number of college-aged people in the United States will fall after 2025, making it easier for people born in the late 2000s and after to get admitted.<ref name="Barshay-2018">{{Cite news |last=Barshay |first=Jill |date=September 10, 2018 |title=College students predicted to fall by more than 15% after the year 2025 |url=https://hechingerreport.org/college-students-predicted-to-fall-by-more-than-15-after-the-year-2025/ |access-date=January 16, 2023 |work=Hechinger Report}}</ref> Indeed, by the mid-2020s, it has already become noticeably easier to get admitted to most colleges and universities in the United States,<ref name=":132">{{Cite news |last=Marcus |first=Jon |date=November 18, 2024 |title=A trend colleges might not want applicants to notice: It's becoming easier to get in |url=https://hechingerreport.org/a-trend-colleges-might-not-want-applicants-to-notice-its-becoming-easier-to-get-in/ |access-date=November 22, 2024 |work=The Hechinger Report}}</ref> though demand for very top American institutions will likely remain more or less unchanged.<ref name="Barshay-2018" /> Institutions address challenges of a small pool of prospective students by dropping programs with low student interest, including many in the liberal arts and the humanities, like [[gender studies]] and [[critical race theory]],<ref name="Dutt-Ballerstadt-2019">{{Cite news |last=Dutt-Ballerstadt |first=Reshmi |date=March 1, 2019 |title=Academic Prioritization or Killing the Liberal Arts? |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/advice/2019/03/01/shrinking-liberal-arts-programs-raise-alarm-bells-among-faculty |access-date=March 1, 2021 |work=Inside Higher Ed}}</ref> and creating majors for emerging fields, such as [[artificial intelligence]],<ref name="Education Dive-2019">{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=November 1, 2019 |title=A look at trends in college and university consolidation since 2016 |url=https://www.educationdive.com/news/how-many-colleges-and-universities-have-closed-since-2016/539379/ |access-date=November 28, 2019 |work=Education Dive}}</ref> or professional programs, such as [[law enforcement]],<ref name="Barshay-2018" /> and investing in online learning programs.<ref name="Education Dive-2019" /> The arrival of [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]] in the United States in 2020 merely accelerated the process.<ref name="The Economist-2020">{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=May 28, 2020 |title=Could a fifth of America's colleges really face the chop? |url=https://www.economist.com/united-states/2020/05/28/could-a-fifth-of-americas-colleges-really-face-the-chop |access-date=July 13, 2020 |newspaper=The Economist |department=United States}}</ref> As a consequence of the economic downturn, families chose to either delay or avoid sending their children to institutions of higher education altogether.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dickler |first=Jessica |date=March 14, 2021 |title=Fewer kids are going to college because they say it costs too much |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/14/fewer-kids-going-to-college-because-of-cost.html |access-date=September 19, 2021 |work=CNBC}}</ref> 
[[File:Majors Change 2011-21.png|center|thumb|680x680px|Most STEM subjects and healthcare grew in popularity while the humanities and the liberal arts have declined due to market forces.<ref name="Dutt-Ballerstadt-2019" />]]
Members of Generation Z are anxious to pick majors that teach them marketable skills,<ref name="Solman-2019" /> with an overwhelming majority consider job preparation to be the point of college.<ref name="WEF-2018">{{Cite web |date=November 30, 2018 |title=Why Generation Z has a totally different approach to money |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2018/11/why-gen-z-is-approaching-money-differently-than-other-generations-95032cb6-6046-4269-a38a-0763bd7909ff/ |access-date=May 15, 2019 |website=World Economic Forum}}</ref> A 2018 Gallup poll on over 32,000 university students randomly selected from 43 schools from across the United States found that just over half (53%) of them thought their chosen major would lead to gainful employment. STEM students expressed the highest confidence (62%) while those in the [[Liberal arts education|liberal arts]] were the least confident (40%). Just over one in three thought they would learn the skills and knowledge needed to become successful in the workplace.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Aucter |first=Zack |date=January 17, 2018 |title=Half of College Students Say Their Major Leads to a Good Job |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/225446/half-college-students-say-major-leads-good-job.aspx |access-date=August 2, 2019 |work=Gallup}}</ref> While the number of students majoring in the humanities has fallen significantly, those in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, or [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]], have risen sharply.<ref name="Solman-2019" /> While about half of STEM graduates work in non-STEM jobs, people with collegiate STEM training still tend to earn more, regardless of whether or not their job is STEM-related or not.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Graf |first1=Nikki |last2=Fry |first2=Richard |last3=Funk |first3=Cary |date=January 9, 2018 |title=7 facts about the STEM workforce |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2018/01/09/7-facts-about-the-stem-workforce/ |access-date=October 26, 2019 |website=Pew Research Center}}</ref>

By the late 2010s, the historical trend of men being more likely to have higher education has reversed. Women are now more likely to enroll in university than men,<ref name="Duffin-2019">{{Cite web |last=Duffin |first=Erin |date=August 9, 2019 |title=Percentage of the U.S. population who have completed four years of college or more from 1940 to 2018, by gender |url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/184272/educational-attainment-of-college-diploma-or-higher-by-gender/ |access-date=October 25, 2019 |website=Statista}}</ref> a trend accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic.<ref name="Belkin-2021" /> By the end of the 2020–21 academic year, 59.5% of university students were women. This growing sex gap has been growing for four decades in the United States in parallel with other countries of middle to high income.<ref name="Belkin-2021" /><ref name="Thompson-2021">{{Cite news |last=Thompson |first=Derek |date=September 14, 2021 |title=Colleges Have a Guy Problem |work=The Atlantic |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/09/young-men-college-decline-gender-gap-higher-education/620066/ |access-date=September 19, 2021 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20210916022128/https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/09/young-men-college-decline-gender-gap-higher-education/620066/ |archive-date=September 16, 2021}}</ref> Among those who attend college or university, women are more likely then men to graduate with a degree within six years.<ref name="Belkin-2021" />

== Health issues ==
=== General ===
A 2020 study of data from 1999 to 2015 suggests that children living with married parents tended to have lower rates of early-life mortality than those living with unmarried or single parents and non-parents.<ref>Rogers, R.G., Hummer, R.A., Tilstra, A.M., Lawrence, E.M. and Mollborn, S. (2020), Family Structure and Early Life Mortality in the United States. ''Journal of Marriage and Family'', 82: 1159-1177. doi:10.1111/jomf.12674</ref>

==== Puberty ====
For girls born in the United States, the average age of the onset of puberty has been steadily falling since the late twentieth century.<ref name=":45">{{Cite news |last=Weil |first=Elizabeth |date=March 30, 2012 |title=Puberty Before Age 10: A New 'Normal'? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/01/magazine/puberty-before-age-10-a-new-normal.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20190504071506/https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/01/magazine/puberty-before-age-10-a-new-normal.html |archive-date=May 4, 2019 |access-date=April 27, 2025 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name="Weir-20162" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last1=Nawaz |first1=Amna |last2=Hudgins |first2=Jackson |title=New study details potential long-term health risks as American girls reach puberty earlier |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/new-study-details-potential-long-term-health-risks-as-american-girls-reach-puberty-earlier |access-date=May 31, 2024 |work=PBS Newshour|date=May 31, 2024}}</ref> According to a 2019 meta-analysis the age of pubertal onset among girls was between 8.8 and 10.3 years in the United States.<ref name="Eckert-Lind-20202">{{Cite journal |last1=Eckert-Lind |first1=Camilla |last2=Busch |first2=Alexander S. |last3=Petersen |first3=Jørgen H. |last4=Biro |first4=Frank M. |last5=Butler |first5=Gary |last6=Bräuner |first6=Elvira V. |last7=Juul |first7=Anders |date=2020 |title=Worldwide Secular Trends in Age at Pubertal Onset Assessed by Breast Development Among Girls: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis |url= |journal=JAMA Pediatrics |publisher=American Medical Association |volume=174 |issue=4 |pages=e195881 |doi=10.1001/jamapediatrics.2019.5881 |pmc=7042934 |pmid=32040143}}</ref> [[Precocious puberty|Early puberty]] is associated with a variety of mental health issues (such as anxiety and depression), early sexual activity, venereal diseases, alcoholism, and substance abuse, among other problems.<ref name=":45" /><ref name="Weir-20162">{{Cite journal |last=Weir |first=Kirsten |date=March 2016 |title=The risks of earlier puberty |url=https://www.apa.org/monitor/2016/03/puberty |journal=Monitor |publisher=American Psychological Association |volume=47 |issue=3 |page=40 |via=}}</ref> Furthermore, factors known for prompting mental health problems—early childhood stress, [[Fatherlessness|absent fathers]], [[Domestic violence|domestic conflict]], and low socioeconomic status—are themselves linked to early pubertal onset.<ref name="Weir-20162" /> According to Dr. Dr. Shruthi Mahalingaiah, [[Body mass index|body-mass index]] is a strong predictor of precocious puberty.<ref name=":2" /> Possible causes of [[Precocious puberty|early puberty]] could be positive, namely improved nutrition,<ref name="Weir-20162" /> or negative, such as obesity, stress, trauma, exposure to [[Endocrine disruptor|hormone-disrupting chemicals]], air pollutants, heavy metals.<ref name="Weir-20162" /><ref name=":2" /> Girls of African ancestry on average enter puberty first, followed by those of Hispanic, European, and Asian extraction, in that order. But African-American girls are less likely to face the negative effects of puberty than their counterparts of European descent.<ref name="Weir-20162" />

=== Physical ===
Data from the NCES showed that in the academic year 2018–19, 15% of students receiving special education under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act was suffering from "other health impairments"—such as [[asthma]], diabetes, epilepsy, heart problems, [[Haemophilia|hemophilia]], lead poisoning, [[leukemia]], nephritis, rheumatic fever, [[Sickle cell disease|sickle cell anemia]], and tuberculosis.<ref name="NCES-2020">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=May 2020|title=Students With Disabilities|url=https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator_cgg.asp|access-date=January 22, 2021|website=National Center for Education Statistics|publisher=Institute of Education Sciences|archive-date=February 21, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200221012459/https://nces.ed.gov/programs/coe/indicator_cgg.asp}}</ref> The [[American Optometric Association]] sounded the alarm on a link between the regular use of handheld electronic devices and eyestrain.<ref name="Stevens-2015">{{Cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/dining/ct-child-vision-problem-computer-balancing-20150716-column.html#nt=standard-embed|title=Too much screen time could be damaging kids' eyesight|last=Stevens|first=Heidi|date=July 16, 2015|work=Chicago Tribune|access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref>

Research by the [[Mayo Clinic]] in Minnesota found [[Food allergy|food allergies]] are becoming increasingly common since the early 2000s. Today, one in twelve American children has a food allergy, with peanut allergy being the most prevalent type.<ref name="The Economist-2019" /> Nut allergies, in general, have quadrupled and shellfish allergies have increased 40% between 2004 and 2019. In all, about 36% of American children have some kind of allergy.<ref name="National Post-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://nationalpost.com/health/why-everybody-is-suddenly-allergic-to-everything|title=Why everybody is suddenly allergic to everything|last=|first=|date=July 30, 2019|work=National Post|access-date=November 24, 2019|department=Health}}</ref> One possible explanation, supported by the [[National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases]], is that parents keep their children "too clean for their own good." According to this "hygiene hypothesis," exposure to allergens give the infant's immune system some exercise, making it less likely to overreact. Evidence for this includes the fact that children living on a farm are consistently less likely to be allergic than their counterparts who are raised in the city, and that children born in a developed country to parents who immigrated from developing nations are more likely to be allergic than their parents are.<ref name="National Post-2019" />

=== Mental ===
A 2018 survey by the American Psychological Association revealed that Generation Z had the weakest mental health of any living generation; some 91% of this demographic cohort reported physical or emotion symptoms associated with stress.<ref name="Piore-2019" /> [[Surgeon General of the United States]] [[Vivek Murthy]] stated in a 2021 advisory that the shares of young people having suicidal ideation and suffering from persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness had grown precipitously compared to the previous decade.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Denworth |first=Lydia |date=July–August 2024 |title=Rx for Teen Mental Health: Volunteering |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/teens-mental-health-may-improve-when-they-help-others/ |journal=Scientific American |volume=331 |issue=1 |pages=85–6 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican072024-2XC13fwbyaWb4QC8Opy1n1 |pmid=39017515 |bibcode=2024SciAm.331a..85D |url-access=subscription }}</ref> There is a growing body of evidence that there is a direct link between having access to social media at a young age and weak mental health,<ref name="Goldfield-2023">{{Cite news |last=Goldfield |first=Gary |date=February 23, 2023 |title=Reducing social media use significantly improves body image in teens, young adults |work=APA Press Releases |publisher=American Psychological Association |url=https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2023/02/social-media-body-image |access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Prinstein-2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Prinstein |first1=Mitchell J. |last2=Telzer |first2=Eva H. |display-authors=1 |date=January 3, 2023 |title=Association of Habitual Checking Behaviors on Social Media With Longitudinal Functional Brain Development |journal=JAMA Pediatrics |publisher=American Medical Association |volume=177 |issue=2 |pages=160–167 |doi=10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.4924|pmid=36595277 |pmc=9857400 }}</ref><ref name="Schwartz-2023" /><ref name="Smyth-2023">{{Cite news |last1=Smyth |first1=Jamie |last2=Murphy |first2=Hannah |date=March 26, 2023 |title=The teen mental health crisis: a reckoning for Big Tech |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/77d06d3e-2b9f-4d46-814f-da2646fea60c |access-date=April 21, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230326051933/https://www.ft.com/content/77d06d3e-2b9f-4d46-814f-da2646fea60c |archive-date=March 26, 2023}}</ref> especially among teenage girls.<ref name=":57">{{Cite journal |last=Shpancer |first=Noam |date=May–June 2023 |title=The State of Youth Mental Health |journal=Psychology Today |page=9}}</ref> Parents who are overly involved in their children's lives are likely making matters worse by preventing their children from developing [[Psychological resilience|emotional resilience]].<ref name=":57" /> Across the United States, university students are seeking mental health support.<ref name="Piore-2019" /> Many are discussing their [[Eco-anxiety|distress over climate change]] with their [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapists]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fagan |first=Abigail |date=January–February 2025 |title=Worrying for the World |url=https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/articles/202501/how-to-cope-when-youre-worrying-for-the-worldlt-today |journal=Psychology Today |pages=39–45}}</ref>

Compared to the 2000s, the 2010s saw a marked increase in the rate of suicide among adolescents, due to an increased willingness by families and coroners to label a death as a result of suicide, depression or opioid usage.<ref name="Miron-2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Miron |first1=Oren |last2=Yu |first2=Kun-Hsing |last3=Wilf-Miron |first3=Rachel |last4=Kohane |first4=Isaac |date=June 18, 2019 |title=Suicide Rates Among Adolescents and Young Adults in the United States, 2000-2017 |journal=JAMA |volume=321 |issue=23 |pages=2362–2364 |doi=10.1001/jama.2019.5054 |pmc=6582264 |pmid=31211337}}</ref> Nadine Kaslow, a psychiatrist and behavioral scientist at the [[Emory University School of Medicine]], pointed to the weakening of familial and other social bonds and the heavy use of modern communications technology, which exposes people to the risk of cyber-bullying.<ref group="note">Also see their [[#Use of information and communications technologies (ICT)|use of information technology]].</ref> The number of American teenagers who exhibited the classic symptoms of [[Depression in childhood and adolescence|depression]] jumped during the 2010s. Psychologist Jean Twenge and her colleagues found that this growth of mental health issues was associated with spending more time in front of a screen. It is not clear, however, whether depression causes a teenager to spend more time online or the other way around. Teens who spent more time online were more likely to not have enough sleep, a major predictor of depression.<ref name="Twenge-2017a">{{Cite news|last=Twenge|first=Jean|date=November 14, 2017|title=With teen mental health deteriorating over five years, there's a likely culprit|work=The Conversation|url=https://theconversation.com/with-teen-mental-health-deteriorating-over-five-years-theres-a-likely-culprit-86996|access-date=November 10, 2020}}</ref> By the mid-2020s, however, the growth of depression and anxiety among young Americans has stalled or slightly reversed, though the reasons remain poorly understood.<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 11, 2025 |title=Young Americans are getting happier |url=https://www.economist.com/united-states/2025/03/11/young-americans-are-getting-happier |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250312152117/https://www.economist.com/united-states/2025/03/11/young-americans-are-getting-happier |archive-date=March 12, 2025 |access-date=June 28, 2025 |newspaper=The Economist}}</ref>

In its analysis of data from the late 2010s, the [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] found that just under half of Americans aged six to seventeen slept for nine hours on most days. Compared to those who did not get enough sleep, those who did were more curious, more likely to finish their homework, and more invested in their education. The risk factors associated with sleep deprivation among children to be the low educational attainment of parents or caregivers, being from families living below the federal poverty line, higher digital media usage, more negative childhood experiences, and mental illnesses.<ref name="AAPed-2019">{{Cite news|last=American Academy of Pediatrics|date=October 25, 2019|title=Only half of US children get enough sleep during the week|work=Science Daily|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/10/191025075604.htm|access-date=November 21, 2020}}</ref> Sleep deprivation is also linked to reduced performance in school and obesity.<ref name="Twenge-2017b">{{Cite news|last=Twenge|first=Jean|date=October 19, 2017|title=Teens are sleeping less – but there's a surprisingly easy fix|work=The Conversation|url=https://theconversation.com/teens-are-sleeping-less-but-theres-a-surprisingly-easy-fix-85157|access-date=November 11, 2020}}</ref> American teenagers share a common habit of having their smartphones on at night, at the expense of the quality of their own sleep.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nadworny |first=Elissa |date=May 15, 2018 |title=Why Teens Should Understand Their Own Brains (And Why Their Teachers Should, Too!) |work=NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/ed/2018/05/15/609769519/why-teenagers-should-understand-their-own-brains-and-why-their-teachers-should-t |access-date=May 13, 2023}}</ref>

There has been some evidence that [[COVID-19 lockdowns]] have accelerated the aging of adolescent brains (as measured by cortical thinning), especially among girls.<ref>{{Cite news |last=University of Washington |date=September 9, 2024 |title=COVID-19 lockdowns prematurely aged teenage brains, study shows |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2024/09/240909160232.htm |access-date=September 30, 2024 |work=Science Daily}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Corrigan |first1=Neva M. |last2=Rokem |first2=Ariel |last3=Kuhl |first3=Patricia K. |date=2024 |title=COVID-19 lockdown effects on adolescent brain structure suggest accelerated maturation that is more pronounced in females than in males |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=121 |issue=38 |article-number=e2403200121 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2403200121|doi-access=free |pmid=39250666 |pmc=11420155 |bibcode=2024PNAS..12103200C }}</ref> According to the [[National Center for Education Statistics]] (NCES), between the academic years 2011–12 and 2018–19, the number of students aged three to twenty-one receiving special education under the [[Individuals with Disabilities Education Act]] (IDEA) increased from 6.4 million to 7.1 million,  one third of whom suffered from a [[specific learning disability]]. After specific learning disabilities, the most common types of learning disorders included [[speech and language impairment]] (19%), autism (11%), and developmental delay (7%).<ref name="NCES-2020" />

Gains in the [[Intelligence quotient|IQ]] scores of Americans first observed during the twentieth century—the [[Flynn effect]]—continued in the early twenty-first century, at least up until 2014.<ref name="Flynn-2018" /> However, [[creativity]] scores, as measured by the [[Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking|Torrance Test of Creative Thinking]], were in decline between the 1990s and the late 2000s. This is partly because American educations have chosen to emphasize standardization and test scores at the expense of encouraging creativity, and because American parents have been allowing their children little play time but a lot of screen time.<ref name="Kim-2011" /><ref>{{Cite news|last1=Bronson|first1=Po|last2=Merryman|first2=Ashley|date=July 10, 2010|title=The Creativity Crisis|work=Newsweek|department=Education|url=https://www.newsweek.com/creativity-crisis-74665|access-date=October 10, 2020}}</ref>

== Political views and participation==
{{Main|Political views of Generation Z}}

=== General trends ===
[[File:Women's March - Washington DC 2017 (32203821400).jpg|thumb|One of the defining moments when the first wave of Generation Z came of age was the [[2017 Women's March]]. Protestors wore their distinctive pink [[pussyhat]]s.]]
In 2018, Gallup found that overall, younger adults tended to lean liberal while older adults tilted conservative.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/245813/leans-conservative-liberals-keep-recent-gains.aspx|title=U.S. Still Leans Conservative, but Liberals Keep Recent Gains|last=Saad|first=Lydia|date=January 8, 2019|work=Gallup Poll|access-date=December 25, 2019|department=Politics}}</ref> Although American voters below the age of 30 are much less likely to identify with the Democratic Party in 2024 than in 2008, youth support for the political left continues to hold during the early 2020s.<ref name=":5">{{Cite news |last=Otis |first=John |date=August 27, 2024 |title=The Gender Gap Among Gen Z Voters, Explained |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/27/insider/the-gender-gap-among-gen-z-voters-explained.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240827221936/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/27/insider/the-gender-gap-among-gen-z-voters-explained.html |archive-date=August 27, 2024 |access-date=September 8, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> However, by 2025, polls consistently show that in terms of political views, Generation Z can be divided into two main groups.<ref name=":22" /><ref name=":58">{{Cite news |last=Pasquini |first=Nina |date=September–October 2025 |title=How MAGA Went Mainstream at Harvard |url=https://www.harvardmagazine.com/students/harvard-young-americans-conservative-turn |access-date=September 13, 2025 |work=Harvard Magazine}}</ref> For the first group, which came of age before the pandemic, the defining political events of their formative years were the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|first term of President Donald Trump]], the [[Women's March#Post-Trump Inauguration marches|Women's March]], the [[Black Lives Matter]] movement, and gun-control demonstrations. This group tends to lean to the left. The second group experienced COVID lockdowns as secondary students and became adults during the [[presidency of Joe Biden]]. This group is noticeably more conservative than the first; for them, the [[Make America Great Again movement]] (MAGA) is [[counterculture]]. They are also more mistrustful of authority.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pandey |first=Erica |date=June 21, 2025 |title=Gen Z's stunning partisan split |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/06/21/gen-z-partisan-split-young-voters |access-date=June 21, 2025 |work=Axios}}</ref>
