But overall, neither group fits neatly into one of the two main political parties of the United States.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":58" /><ref name=":64" /> In fact, they largely distrust them<ref name=":64" /> and generally expect more substantive information on policies before casting their vote.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Moore |first=Elena |date=February 6, 2023 |title=Gen Z's political power: new data gives insight into America's youngest voters |work=NPR |url=https://www.npr.org/2023/02/06/1154172568/gen-zs-political-power-new-data-gives-insight-into-americas-youngest-voters |access-date=February 7, 2023}}</ref> While some of the key issues for this cohort are climate change, gender equality, reproductive rights, and gun violence,<ref name=":7" /> economic concerns are the most important ones for Generation Z, especially [[2021–2023 inflation surge|inflation]], the cost of housing, income inequality, and taxes.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |date=September 19, 2024 |title=What are we getting wrong about young voters?, with Cathy Cohen (Ep. 142) |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/what-are-we-getting-wrong-about-young-voters |website=Big Brains |publisher=University of Chicago}}</ref> Among college students, the top issues are healthcare reforms, the cost of education, and civil rights.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Habeshian |first=Sareen |date=May 7, 2024 |title=Exclusive poll: Most college students shrug at nationwide protests |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/05/07/poll-students-israel-hamas-protests |access-date=May 28, 2024 |work=Axios}}</ref> Most do not care about Middle Eastern conflicts and the associated protests on college campuses,<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":9" /> but are more interested in lucrative careers after graduation.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Mari |first=Francesca |date=May 22, 2024 |title=What Do Students at Elite Colleges Really Want? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/22/business/gen-z-college-students-jobs.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240523044217/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/22/business/gen-z-college-students-jobs.html |archive-date=May 23, 2024 |access-date=May 28, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Among young men, a majority think that both parties hold extreme views, but that the Republican Party is more so than the Democratic Party.<ref name=":35">{{Cite web |last1=Morris |first1=G. Elliott |last2=Druke |first2=Galen |date=October 30, 2024 |title=How will young men vote in the 2024 election? |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lblJEM5F_LM |website=538 Politics Podcast}}</ref> Being disappointed at the status quo has been an impetus for them to run for office, taking advantage of the fact that a majority of voters would like to see younger faces in politics.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Rubin |first=April |date=June 29, 2025 |title=Gen Z and millennials push into politics |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/06/29/gen-z-millennials-elections-zohran-mamdani |access-date=June 29, 2025 |work=Axios}}</ref>

Social media networks have played a crucial role in how members Generation Z form and share their political views.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":39">{{Cite news |last=Hinckley |first=Story |date=September 27, 2024 |title=Young women and men are diverging on politics. Why this gender gap matters. |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/USA/Politics/2024/0927/gender-gap-trump-harris-youth-vote |access-date=October 31, 2024 |work=Christian Science Monitor}}</ref> The algorithms of these platforms typically serve contents that reinforce the views of the user and help them mind other like-minded individuals.<ref name=":43">{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=Claire Cain |date=September 15, 2024 |title=How the Last Eight Years Made Young Women More Liberal |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/15/upshot/election-young-women-liberal.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240916140744/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/15/upshot/election-young-women-liberal.html |archive-date=September 16, 2024 |access-date=November 5, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> There is evidence that TikTok has led to the rightward shift of Generation Z.<ref name=":22" /> On the other hand, it has also brought Representative [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]] to the attention of many Gen-Z women.<ref name=":43" /> Compared to older cohorts, Generation Z as a group is more skeptical of the American federal government and less concerned about the possible risks to national security posed by TikTok; many oppose the proposed TikTok ban.<ref name="Sherman-2023" /> As a result, politicians from both major political parties have been trying to appeal to young voters on social networks, including TikTok itself.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Vinall |first=Frances |date=August 20, 2025 |title=White House creates account on TikTok, the app Trump once tried to ban |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/08/20/trump-white-house-tiktok-account/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250820094034/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/08/20/trump-white-house-tiktok-account/ |archive-date=August 20, 2025 |access-date=November 26, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref>

Generation Z's political views have also been shaped by the way they are taught history. Changes to the curriculum of American history during the 2010s, especially in left-leaning states, have led to large numbers young Americans having a low opinion of their country and their historical figures. On the other hand, the decline of belief in American exceptionalism is a long-term trend, not unique to this cohort.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Twenge |first=Jean |date=October 25, 2024 |title=The Death of American exceptionalism |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2024/10/youth-democracy-united-states-unique/680344/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241025111800/https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2024/10/youth-democracy-united-states-unique/680344/ |archive-date=October 25, 2024 |access-date=October 25, 2024 |work=The Atlantic}}</ref>

=== Sex differences ===
There are significant sex differences in political views among Generation Z, with young women under 30 years of age being broadly left-wing and young men being right-leaning on a variety of issues from immigration to sexual harassment.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite news |last=Burn-Murdoch |first=John |date=January 26, 2024 |title=A new global gender divide is emerging |url=https://www.ft.com/content/29fd9b5c-2f35-41bf-9d4c-994db4e12998 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240126143811/https://www.ft.com/content/29fd9b5c-2f35-41bf-9d4c-994db4e12998 |archive-date=January 26, 2024 |access-date=January 26, 2024 |work=Financial Times}}</ref> A gender gap has been observed since [[1980 United States presidential election|1980]], when women were more likely to vote for the Democratic Party and men for the Republican Party. But this gap has widened during the 2010s and 2020s.<ref name=":41">{{Cite news |last1=Kamarck |first1=Elaine |last2=Muchnick |first2=Jordan |date=May 23, 2024 |title=The growing gender gap among young people |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-growing-gender-gap-among-young-people/ |access-date=October 31, 2024 |work=Brookings Institution}}</ref> 

According to Gallup, the gap as of early 2024 among voters below the age of 30 was 30 percentage points.<ref name=":6" /> Some young men believe that [[Feminist movement|women's progress]] has come at their expense, that it should be acceptable to discuss men's mental health issues, that men's economic concerns have not been addressed, or that most politicians have ignored them.<ref name=":18">{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=Claire Cain |date=August 24, 2024 |title=Many Gen Z Men Feel Left Behind. Some See Trump as an Answer. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/24/upshot/trump-polls-young-men.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240829033104/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/24/upshot/trump-polls-young-men.html |archive-date=August 29, 2024 |access-date=September 8, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name=":19">{{Cite news |last=Wendling |first=Mike |date=October 11, 2024 |title=Trump talks MMA and golf in podcast push for young male voters |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cj9j43890k7o |access-date=October 11, 2024 |work=BBC News}}</ref> Facing despair and political homelessness, many young men find [[Donald Trump]] an appealing alternative.<ref name=":41" /><ref name=":19" /> 

In contrast, many young women became politically active because of the [[Hillary Clinton 2016 presidential campaign|2016 presidential campaign]] of Secretary of State [[Hillary Clinton]], the [[MeToo movement|me-too]] movement, the ''[[Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization|Dobbs v. Jackson]]'' decision on abortion by the Supreme Court, and the [[Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign|2024 presidential campaign]] of Vice President [[Kamala Harris]] (after incumbent President [[Joe Biden]] announced he would not seek re-election).<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=Claire Cain |date=August 24, 2024 |title=These Young Women Didn't Want to Vote for Biden. They're All In on Harris. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/24/upshot/harris-polling-young-women.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240824100326/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/24/upshot/harris-polling-young-women.html |archive-date=August 24, 2024 |access-date=September 8, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name=":43" /> In fact, Harris managed to secure the support of many young female voters, who previously only reluctantly voted for Biden or did not vote at all,<ref name=":39" /> and her support among women has been rising faster than among young men.<ref name=":19" /> 

Another reason for the gender gap is the fact that young women are better educated and earning more than men in the contemporary American economy.<ref name=":41" /><ref name=":33">{{Cite news |last=Kay |first=Kathy |date=October 27, 2024 |title=What's really behind America's men v women election |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cjr430gry81o |access-date=October 27, 2024 |work=BBC News}}</ref> In all, American women below the age of 30 have been moving leftward on a number of key political issues while young men have not moved as much.<ref name=":43" /> There is little to no gap in terms of educational attainment or race.<ref name=":39" /> Meanwhile, a majority of Gen Z men are engaging with contents from "[[Manosphere|masculinity influencers]]" on the Internet, who promote traditional gender roles in which men make the decisions and women comply.<ref name=":65" />

=== Elections ===
[[File:You're Being Brainwashed tour attendees (54034592443).jpg|thumb|Young Americans, seen here with their MAGA hats, have been turning towards the right since 2020.]]
As more and more members of Generation Z reached adulthood during the 2020s, voter turnouts in this cohort has been growing, even though young people are still less likely to vote than older generations. In particular, political participation among young women has jumped, breaking a historical trend in which young men were more likely to vote.<ref name=":7" /> Living in an age of political polarization has motivated this cohort to participate in the political process.<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> A survey conducted before the 2020 U.S. presidential election by [[Barnes & Noble|Barnes and Noble Education]] on 1,500 college students nationwide found that just one third of respondents believe who they vote for is "private information" and three quarters of them find it difficult to find unbiased news sources.<ref name="Business Wire-2019" />

[[2018 United States elections|2018]] was the first year when the majority of voters aged 18 to 24 were members of Generation Z,<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> and they cast 4% of the votes.<ref>{{Cite web|date=May 29, 2019|title=Gen Z, Millennials and Gen X outvoted older generations in 2018 midterms|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2019/05/29/gen-z-millennials-and-gen-x-outvoted-older-generations-in-2018-midterms/|access-date=June 10, 2019|website=Pew Research Center}}</ref> During the [[2020 United States presidential election|2020 U.S. presidential election]], Millennials and Generation Z voted for Joe Biden by a margin of 20 percentage points. Generation Z cast 8% of the votes that year.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Igielnik |first1=Ruth |last2=Keeter |first2=Scott |last3=Hartig |first3=Hannah |date=June 30, 2021 |title=Behind Biden's 2020 Victory |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/06/30/behind-bidens-2020-victory/ |access-date=November 1, 2024 |work=Pew Research Center}}</ref> High youth turnout was a factor behind Biden's victory.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pandey |first=Erica |date=November 7, 2024 |title=A big chunk of the future electorate is MAGA red |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/11/07/young-men-voters-trump-2024-exit-polls |access-date=May 10, 2025 |work=Axios}}</ref> Yet, young people's support for him fell quickly afterwards. By late 2021, only 29% of adults in this age group approved of his performance as president whereas 50% disapproved, a gap of 21 points, the largest of all age groups.<ref>{{Cite news|date=December 16, 2021|title=Young Americans are souring on Joe Biden|newspaper=The Economist|department=Daily Chart|url=https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2021/12/16/young-americans-are-souring-on-joe-biden|access-date=January 5, 2022|archive-url=https://archive.today/20211216233426/https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2021/12/16/young-americans-are-souring-on-joe-biden|archive-date=December 16, 2021}}</ref> In the [[2022 United States elections|2022 midterm election]], voters below the age of 30 were the only major age group supporting the Democratic Party, but their numbers still were large enough to prevent Republicans from controlling the majority of seats in the Senate.<ref name="Barinka-2023">{{Cite news |last=Barinka |first=Alex |date=January 23, 2023 |title=TikTok Bans at Major Colleges Aren't Going Over Well With Students |work=Bloomberg |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2023-01-23/tiktok-bans-at-college-aren-t-going-over-well-with-students |access-date=January 23, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230123182426/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2023-01-23/tiktok-bans-at-college-aren-t-going-over-well-with-students |archive-date=January 23, 2023}}</ref> In the [[2024 United States presidential election|2024 presidential election]], Americans aged 18 to 29 voted for Kamala Harris by a margin of only four points, according to exit polls conducted by the Associated Press.<ref>{{Cite news |last=News Desk |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Interactive: How key groups of Americans voted in 2024 |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/interactive-how-key-groups-of-americans-voted-in-2024-according-to-ap-votecast |access-date=November 12, 2024 |work=PBS News Hour}}</ref> Donald Trump and his Republican Party made considerable gains among young voters, especially young men and European Americans.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 7, 2024 |title=Overall Youth Turnout Down From 2020 But Strong in Battleground States |url=https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-research/overall-youth-turnout-down-2020-strong-battleground-states |work=Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) |publisher=Jonathan M. Tisch College of Civic Life, [[Tufts University]]}}</ref> Among Gen-Z women, while those of ethnic-minority backgrounds overwhelmingly supported Harris, those of European ancestry were evenly split between Harris and Trump.<ref name=":22" /> This election has broken the historical trend of young people generally voting for Democrats. Generation Z has been shifting towards the right since 2020.<ref name=":42">{{Cite news |last=Hill |first=Faith |date=November 4, 2024 |title=The Myth of Woke Gen Z |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/family/archive/2024/11/gen-z-woke-myth-election/680653/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241114165602/https://www.theatlantic.com/family/archive/2024/11/gen-z-woke-myth-election/680653/ |archive-date=November 14, 2024 |access-date=April 24, 2024 |work=The Atlantic}}</ref><ref name=":44">{{Cite news |last=Adeosun |first=Adeola |date=March 22, 2025 |title=Democratic Pollster 'Shocked' At Gen Z's Conservative Shift |url=https://www.newsweek.com/democratic-pollster-shocked-gen-z-conservative-shift-2049107 |access-date=April 24, 2025 |work=Newsweek}}</ref> Even so, polls conducted after that election showed that the majority of Generation Z disapproved of the performance of President Donald Trump because he had failed to address their concerns about the economy, especially inflation and the cost of living.<ref>{{Cite news |last=MacHardy |first=Martha |date=April 28, 2025 |title=Is Gen Z Abandoning Donald Trump? |url=https://www.newsweek.com/donald-trump-approval-rating-gen-z-polling-2060330 |access-date=April 30, 2025 |work=Newsweek}}</ref><ref name=":64">{{Cite news |last=Marcus |first=Josh |date=December 29, 2025 |title=Gen Z men are moving away from MAGA in droves, polls show |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/gen-z-maga-2026-poll-b2891778.html |access-date=December 31, 2025 |work=The Independent}}</ref>

=== Trust in the institutions ===
In 2019, the Pew Research Center interviewed over 2,000 Americans aged 18 and over on their views of various components of the federal government. They found that 54% of the people between the ages of 18 and 29 wanted larger government compared to 43% who preferred smaller government and fewer services. Older people were more likely to pick the second option.<ref group="note">Overall, the American people remained divided over the size and scope of government, with 48% preferring smaller government with fewer services and 46% larger government and more services. Pew found that the most popular federal agencies were the [[United States Postal Service|U.S. Postal Service]] (90% favorable), the [[National Park Service]] (86%), [[NASA]] (81%), the CDC (80%), the FBI (70%), the [[United States Census Bureau|Census Bureau]] (69%), the [[Social Security Administration|SSA]] (66%), the CIA, and the Federal Reserve (both 65%). There was very little to no partisan divide on the Postal Service, the National Park Service, NASA, the CIA, or the Census Bureau.</ref><ref name="fed-trust">{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=October 1, 2019|title=Public Expresses Favorable Views of a Number of Federal Agencies|work=Pew Research Center|department=U.S. Politics & Policy|url=https://www.people-press.org/2019/10/01/public-expresses-favorable-views-of-a-number-of-federal-agencies/|access-date=January 4, 2020}}</ref> 2018 polls conducted by the Pew Research Center found that 70% of Americans aged 13 to 17 wanted the government to play a more active role in solving their problems.<ref name="Pew-2019b" />

A 2022 poll by Pew showed that overall, medical experts, the military, and scientists were among the most trusted groups in the United States. But while a majority of Americans believed it was important for their country to remain a global leader in science, people aged 18 to 29 were somewhat less inclined to think so compared to older cohorts and were slightly more optimistic about the standing of U.S. science on the international stage.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Kennedy |first1=Brian |last2=Tyson |first2=Alec |last3=Funk |first3=Carrie |date=October 25, 2022 |title=Americans Value U.S. Role as Scientific Leader, but 38% Say Country Is Losing Ground Globally |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2022/10/25/americans-value-u-s-role-as-scientific-leader-but-38-say-country-is-losing-ground-globally/ |access-date=December 27, 2022 |website=Pew Research Center}}</ref> However, Generation Z's trust in institutions or the nation itself has been declining.<ref name=":63" /> Polls conducted during the early 2020s showed that only a minority of Americans aged 18–29 thought that their country was heading in the right direction or agreed that democracy was the best form of government.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 9, 2024 |title=Gen Z doesn't believe in government. The solution is closer to home than you think. |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/voices/2024/12/09/local-government-elections-gen-z-vote/76794946007/ |first=David|last=Millman |access-date=December 13, 2024 |work= USA Today |department=U.S. Politics & Policy}}</ref> About two thirds did not trust their government.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Romei |first1=Valentina |last2=Munir |first2=Zehra |date=March 17, 2025 |title=Young Americans lose trust in the state |url=https://www.ft.com/content/44a7927b-66d7-4321-8425-08ed162a3994 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250318132043/https://www.ft.com/content/44a7927b-66d7-4321-8425-08ed162a3994 |archive-date=March 18, 2025 |access-date=April 24, 2024 |work=Financial Times}}</ref>

=== Gun ownership ===
[[File:US gun ownership.png|frameless|263x263px|left]]
The [[March for Our Lives]], a protest taking place in the aftermath of the [[Stoneman Douglas High School shooting]] in 2018 was described by various media outlets as being led by students and young people. Some even describe it as the political "awakening" of Generation Z or that these protesters were "the voice of a generation on gun control."<ref>{{cite news|last1=Wierson|first1=Arick|date=23 March 2018|title=March for our Lives gun control rally only hints at the political power of Generation Z|publisher=CNBC|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/03/23/march-for-our-lives-gun-control-rally-only-hints-at-the-political-power-of-generation-z.html|access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Anapol|first1=Avery|date=14 March 2018|title=NJ student march organizers pen op-ed to NRA We Wont Let You Win|work=The Hill|url=https://thehill.com/blogs/blog-briefing-room/378333-nj-student-march-organizers-pen-op-ed-to-nra-we-wont-let-you-win/|access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=13 March 2018|title=Dear National Rifle Association: We Won't Let You Win. From, Teenagers.|work=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/13/opinion/nra-shooting-marjory-stoneman-douglas.html|access-date=24 March 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Wallheiser|first=Mark|date=February 20, 2018|title=What's different now? Parkland students won't let us get away with no action on guns.|url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/news-columns-blogs/fabiola-santiago/article201179124.html|access-date=June 9, 2019|website=Miami Herald}}</ref> While this massive protest was indeed organized by the survivors of the Parkland shooting, albeit with the assistance of well-resourced and older benefactors, the reality was a little more complicated.<ref name="Fisher-2018">{{Cite news|last=Fisher|first=Dana|date=28 March 2018|title=Here's who actually attended the March for Our Lives. (No, it wasn't mostly young people.)|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/wp/2018/03/28/heres-who-actually-attended-the-march-for-our-lives-no-it-wasnt-mostly-young-people|access-date=20 January 2019}}</ref> According to a field survey by ''The Washington Post'' interviewing every fifth person at the protest, only ten percent of the participants were 18 years of age or younger. Meanwhile, the adult participants of the protest had an average age of just under 49.<ref name="Fisher-2018" /> Polls conducted by Gallup and the Pew Research Center found that support for stricter gun laws among people aged 18 to 29 and 18 to 36, respectively, is statistically no different from that of the general population. According to Gallup, 57% of Americans are in favor of stronger gun control legislation.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 24, 2018|title=Millennials Are No More Liberal On Gun Control Than Elders, Polls Show|url=https://www.npr.org/2018/02/24/588069946/millennials-are-no-more-liberal-on-gun-control-than-elders-polls-show|access-date=June 9, 2019|website=NPR}}</ref> In a 2017 poll, Pew found that among the age group 18 to 29, 27% personally owned a gun and 16% lived with a gun owner, for a total of 43% living in a household with at least one gun. Nationwide, a similar percentage of American adults lived in a household with a gun. (See chart.)<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Parker|first1=Kim|last2=Horowitz|first2=Julianna Menasce|last3=Igielnik|first3=Ruth|last4=Oliphant|first4=J. Baxter|last5=Brown|first5=Anna|date=June 22, 2017|title=America's Complex Relationship With Guns|work=Pew Research Center|department=Social Trends|url=https://www.pewsocialtrends.org/2017/06/22/americas-complex-relationship-with-guns/|access-date=November 13, 2019}}</ref>

=== Economics and the environment ===
[[File:View_on_Climate_Change.png|alt=|470x470px|right]]
Harvard University's Institute of Politics Youth Poll from 2019 found that support for [[Single-payer healthcare|single-payer universal healthcare]] and tuition-free free college dropped, down 8% to 47% and down 5% to 51%, respectively, if cost estimates were provided.<ref name="KennedyInst-2019">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=April 22, 2019|title=Spring 2019 Harvard IOP Youth Poll Results|url=https://iop.harvard.edu/about/newsletter-press-release/spring-2019-harvard-iop-youth-poll-results|access-date=September 14, 2019|website=Harvard Kennedy School Institute of Politics}}</ref> According to the [[Hispanic Heritage Foundation]], about eight out of ten members of Generation Z identify as "[[Fiscal conservatism|fiscal conservatives]]."<ref name="HuffPo-2017">{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=October 20, 2017 |title=Conservative or Liberal? For Generation Z, It's Not That Simple |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/conservative-or-liberal-its-not-that-simple-with_b_59ea34f7e4b034105edd4e32?guccounter=1 |access-date=May 12, 2019 |work=Huffington Post}}</ref> In 2018, the [[International Federation of Accountants]] released a report on a survey of 3,388 individuals aged 18 to 23 hailing from G20 countries, with a sample size of 150 to 300 per country. They found that healthcare is a top priority for Generation Z in Canada, France, Germany, and the United States.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |date=2019 |title=Identifying What Matters Most to the Next Generation |url=https://www.ifac.org/system/files/uploads/PPRAG/IFAC_GenZ_Report_FINAL.pdf |access-date=July 10, 2019 |website=International Federation of Accountants}}</ref>

Surveys conducted in the late 2010s and early 2020s indicated that majorities of Generation Z believed that climate change was real and was caused by human activities.<ref name="Pew-2019b" /><ref name=":17">{{Cite news |last1=De Pinto |first1=Jennifer |last2=Backus |first2=Fred |date=September 15, 2019 |title=Younger Americans views' on climate change: More serious, yet more optimistic |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/younger-americans-views-on-climate-change-more-serious-yet-more-optimistic/ |access-date=September 15, 2019 |work=CBS News}}</ref> Differences in opinion might be due to education as younger Americans are more likely to have been taught about climate change in schools than their elders.<ref name=":17" /> Moreover, Generation Z broadly supports the United States transitioning away from fossil fuels and towards ([[Generation IV reactor|next-generation]]) nuclear reactors and [[Renewable energy in the United States|renewable energy]]. Majorities of this cohort also favored [[Carbon capture and storage|carbon capture]] and a ban on Arctic drilling.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Brown |first=H. Claire |date=August 12, 2024 |title=Gen Z Voters Support Climate Action and Nuclear Energy, Poll Finds |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/gen-z-voters-support-climate-action-and-nuclear-energy-poll-finds-26d93950 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240814094617/https://www.wsj.com/articles/gen-z-voters-support-climate-action-and-nuclear-energy-poll-finds-26d93950 |archive-date=August 14, 2024 |access-date=October 11, 2024 |work=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref>

A 2018 Gallup poll found that people aged 18 to 29 have a more favorable view of [[Socialism in the United States|socialism]] than capitalism, 51% to 45%. Older Americans consistently prefer capitalism to socialism.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Newport|first=Frank|date=August 13, 2018|title=Democrats More Positive About Socialism Than Capitalism|url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/240725/democrats-positive-socialism-capitalism.aspx|access-date=May 16, 2019|newspaper=Gallup.com}}</ref>

=== Abortion, sexuality, and family values ===
In 2016, the [[Varkey Foundation]] and [[Populus Ltd|Populus]] conducted an international study examining the attitudes of 20,000 people aged 15 to 21 in twenty countries. They found that just under two thirds of young Americans favored keeping abortion legal, in line with the global average.<ref name="Broadbent-2017">{{cite news|last1=Broadbent|first1=Emma|last2=Gougoulis|first2=John|last3=Lui|first3=Nicole|last4=Pota|first4=Vikas|last5=Simons|first5=Jonathan|date=January 2017|title=Generation Z: Global Citizenship Survey|work=|publisher=[[Varkey Foundation]]|url=https://www.varkeyfoundation.org/media/4487/global-young-people-report-single-pages-new.pdf|access-date=November 15, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820230036/https://www.varkeyfoundation.org/media/4487/global-young-people-report-single-pages-new.pdf}}</ref> Gallup polls conducted in 2019 revealed that 62% of people aged 18 to 29—older members of Generation Z and younger Millennials—support giving women access to [[Abortion in the United States|abortion]] while 33% opposed. At the national level, Americans are split on the issue of abortion.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/244709/pro-choice-pro-life-2018-demographic-tables.aspx|title="Pro-Choice" or "Pro-Life," 2018 Demographic Table|last=|first=|date=2019|website=Gallup|access-date=November 16, 2019}}</ref> Many participants in the annual [[March for Life (Washington, D.C.)|March for Life in Washington, D.C.]] in the early 2020s are members of Generation Z.<ref name="Morrow-2020">{{cite news|last1=Morrow|first1=Brendan|date=January 23, 2020|title=Young anti-abortion marchers look forward to 'post-Roe America'|work=[[The Guardian]]|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/jan/23/young-anti-abortion-marchers-washington-march-for-life|access-date=January 24, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last1=Mullen|first1=Michelle|last2=Lai|first2=Man Sum|date=January 22, 2022|title=Gen Z marchers praying for an end to US abortion|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/av/world-us-canada-60088680|access-date=January 25, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Paz|first=Christian|date=January 24, 2022|title=The Anti-abortion Movement's Gen-Z Victors|work=The Atlantic|department=Politics|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2022/01/march-for-life-abortion-protest/621349/|access-date=January 25, 2022|archive-url=https://archive.today/20220124185546/https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2022/01/march-for-life-abortion-protest/621349/|archive-date=January 24, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="McDaniel-2023">{{Cite news |last1=McDaniel |first1=Justine |last2=Kitchener |first2=Caroline |last3=Boorstein |first3=Michelle |date=January 20, 2023 |title=With Roe dead, thousands attend March for Life in Washington |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/01/20/abortion-march-for-life-2023/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230121171931/https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/01/20/abortion-march-for-life-2023/ |archive-date=January 21, 2023}}</ref> However, there is a sex gap in which Gen Z men are significantly less likely to support legal abortion than women and do not think of restrictions on reproductive choices as something important.<ref name=":65">{{Cite news |last=Varney |first=Sarah |last2=Wellford |first2=Rachel |date=April 21, 2026 |title=Gen Z men and women on why they're sharply divided over reproductive rights |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/gen-z-men-and-women-on-why-theyre-sharply-divided-over-reproductive-rights |access-date=April 21, 2026 |work=PBS Newshour}}</ref>[[File:Abortion Views 2019.png|alt=|center]]A 2018 poll conducted by [[Harris Insights & Analytics|Harris]] on behalf of the LGBT advocacy group [[GLAAD]] found that despite being frequently described as the most tolerant segment of society, people aged 18 to 34—most Millennials and the oldest members of Generation Z—have become less accepting of LGBT individuals compared to previous years.<ref name="Miller-2019a">{{Cite news |last=Miller |first=Susan |date=June 24, 2019 |title=The young are regarded as the most tolerant generation. That's why results of this LGBTQ survey are 'alarming' |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2019/06/24/lgbtq-acceptance-millennials-decline-glaad-survey/1503758001/ |access-date=December 26, 2019 |work=USA Today |department=Nation}}</ref> 
[[File:Discomfort_with_LGBT.png|alt=|center]]

2018 surveys of teenagers 13 to 17 and adults aged 18 or over conducted by the Pew Research Center found that Generation Z has broadly similar views to the Millennials on various political and social issues.  67% were indifferent towards pre-nuptial cohabitation. 49% considered single motherhood to be neither a positive nor a negative for society. 62% saw increased ethnic or racial diversity as good for society. As did 48% for same-sex marriage, and 53% for interracial marriage. In most cases, Generation Z and the Millennials tended to hold different views from the Silent Generation, while the Baby Boomers and Generation X were in between. In the case of financial responsibility in a two-parent household, though, majorities from across the generations answered that it should be shared, with 58% for the Silent Generation, 73% for the Baby Boomers, 78% for Generation X, and 79% for both the Millennials and Generation Z. Across all the generations surveyed, at least 84% thought that both parents ought to be responsible for rearing children. About 13% of Generation Z thought that mothers should be the primary caretaker of children, with similar percentages for the other demographic cohorts. Very few thought that fathers should be the ones mainly responsible for taking care of children.<ref name="Pew-2019b">{{Cite web|url=http://www.pewsocialtrends.org/2019/01/17/generation-z-looks-a-lot-like-millennials-on-key-social-and-political-issues/|title=Generation Z Looks a Lot Like Millennials on Key Social and Political Issues|last=|first=|date=January 17, 2019|website=Pew Research Center|language=en-US|access-date=November 10, 2019}}</ref> Pew, however, noted that the views of this demographic cohort could change in the future as they age and due to new events. Even so, they could play a significant role in the shaping of the political landscape.<ref name="Pew Research Center-2018b" />[[File:Same-sex Marriage Generational Attitudes.png|alt=|center]]A 2023 poll by ''The Wall Street Journal'' and the National Opinion Research Center (NORC) at the University of Chicago found that about 23% of people adults below the age of 30 thought that having children was important, 9 percentage points below those aged 65 and above.<ref name="Zitner-2023" />

=== Immigration ===
[[File:Youths'_Views_on_Legal_Migration.png|center|660x660px]]
In a 2016 survey conducted by the Varkey Foundation and Populus, the question of whether or not those 15 to 21 favored legal migration received mixed responses. In the United States, that margin of support was 16%, higher than the global average of 8%. (See chart above.)<ref name="Weale-2017">{{cite news|last=Weale|first=Sally|date=8 February 2017|title=UK second only to Japan for young people's poor mental wellbeing|work=[[The Guardian]]|url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2017/feb/08/uk-second-japan-young-people-poor-mental-wellbeing|access-date=18 April 2018}}</ref><ref name="Broadbent-2017a">{{cite news|last1=Broadbent|first1=Emma|last2=Gougoulis|first2=John|last3=Lui|first3=Nicole|last4=Pota|first4=Vikas|last5=Simons|first5=Jonathan|date=January 2017|title=Generation Z: Global Citizenship Survey|publisher=[[Varkey Foundation]]|url=https://www.varkeyfoundation.org/media/4487/global-young-people-report-single-pages-new.pdf|access-date=November 15, 2019|archive-date=August 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190820230036/https://www.varkeyfoundation.org/media/4487/global-young-people-report-single-pages-new.pdf}}</ref> According to Gallup, Americans aged 18 to 34 are more likely to view immigration as a "good thing" than their elders.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Saad |first=Lydia |date=August 8, 2022 |title=U.S. Immigration Views Remain Mixed and Highly Partisan |url=https://news.gallup.com/poll/395882/immigration-views-remain-mixed-highly-partisan.aspx |access-date=January 16, 2023 |website=Gallup}}</ref> By 2024, a clear majority of young adults supported increased patrols along the American-Mexican border to combat illegal immigration into the United States.<ref name=":54" />

=== Foreign policy ===
Polls conducted in the late 2010s and early 2020s of adults under the age of 30 show that the top foreign-policy issues for this cohort were combating climate change, preventing the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and defending the United States from terrorism.<ref name="KennedyInst-2019" /><ref name=":14">{{Cite news |last1=Hattfield |first1=Jenn |last2=Silver |first2=Laura |date=July 19, 2024 |title=U.S. adults under 30 have different foreign policy priorities than older adults |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/07/19/us-adults-under-30-have-different-foreign-policy-priorities-than-older-adults/ |access-date=September 29, 2024 |work=Pew Research Center}}</ref> Maintaining American military strength and defending American allies were not as important to young voters.<ref name=":14" /> Moreover, young Americans are markedly less concerned about [[Second Cold War|combating America's geopolitical adversaries]], notably China and Russia, compared to older voters, who still have lingering sentiments from the (previous) [[Cold War]].<ref name=":14" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=March 23, 2023 |title=Younger Americans are friendlier to China |url=https://www.economist.com/united-states/2023/03/23/younger-americans-are-friendlier-to-china |archive-url=https://archive.today/20230323153105/https://www.economist.com/united-states/2023/03/23/younger-americans-are-friendlier-to-china |archive-date=March 23, 2023 |access-date=April 3, 2023 |newspaper=The Economist}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Silver |first1=Laura |last2=Huang |first2=Christine |last3=Clancy |first3=Laura |last4=Fagan |first4=Moira |date=April 12, 2023 |title=Americans Are Critical of China's Global Role – as Well as Its Relationship With Russia |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2023/04/12/americans-are-critical-of-chinas-global-role-as-well-as-its-relationship-with-russia/ |access-date=April 16, 2023 |publisher=Pew Research Center}}</ref> A 2019 poll by the International Federation of Accountants found that in the United States, 52% of Generation Z wanted their government to focus more on national problems, a 24% margin ahead of those who thought otherwise.<ref name=":16" /> Similarly, 2020 poll conducted by the Center for American Progress found that only 18% of Americans supported [[liberal internationalism]], which has been part of American foreign policy since the time of President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]], while young Americans were even less likely to support it, contributing to a return towards [[United States non-interventionism|isolationism]], a historical norm dating back to the [[Founding Fathers of the United States|Founding Fathers]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Kupchan|first=Charles A.|date=September 27, 2020|title=Isolationism Is Not a Dirty Word|work=The Atlantic|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2020/09/virtue-isolationism/616499/|access-date=September 5, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210902154310/https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2020/09/virtue-isolationism/616499/|archive-date=September 2, 2021}}</ref> Polls indicates that by 2025, there is broad support for isolationism and tariffs (imposed by President Donald Trump in his [[Tariffs in the second Trump administration|trade wars]]) among Gen-Z Americans.<ref name=":58" /> One by the [[Carnegie Endowment for International Peace]] found that although American Zoomers were not averse to international engagements, they preferred a more modest role for the United States in global affairs, including in dealing with China, Israel, and Ukraine.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Gen Z Thinks About U.S. Foreign Policy |url=https://carnegieendowment.org/research/2025/04/generation-z-american-foreign-policy-poll?lang=en |access-date=2025-12-02 |website=Carnegie Endowment for International Peace |language=en}}</ref> (See the [[Second Cold War]], Israel's [[War in Gaza]], and the [[Russo-Ukrainian war|Russo-Ukrainian War]].) 

==Religious tendencies==
{{See also|Religion in the United States}}[[File:Views on Religion (Barna 2016).png|border|center]]
Although [[Christianity in the United States|Christianity]] remains the single most popular religion in the United States, [[secularism]] has been growing thanks to Millennials and Generation Z.<ref name="Jones-2022" /><ref name=":46" /> Among adults born between 2000 and 2006, only about a quarter prayed daily or attended religious service at least once a month.<ref name=":53">{{Cite web |last1=Smith |first1=Gregory A. |last2=Cooperman |first2=Alan |display-authors=1 |date=February 26, 2025 |title=Decline of Christianity in the U.S. Has Slowed, May Have Leveled Off |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/decline-of-christianity-in-the-us-has-slowed-may-have-leveled-off/ |access-date=June 13, 2025 |website=Pew Research Center}}</ref> About twenty-nine percent were religiously unaffiliated.<ref name=":46">{{Cite news |last=Contreras |first=Russell |date=November 13, 2025 |title=U.S. faith levels plummet to lowest on record |url=https://www.axios.com/2025/11/13/gallup-us-religion-plunge-shift-global-declines |access-date=December 30, 2025 |work=Axios}}</ref> Americans who came of age during the 2020s were much more likely to have been raised in secular households. About three quarters of those who grew up in such an environment continued to be irreligious. Among those raised in highly religious households, just under a third still attended religious services regularly or thought of religion as important in their lives.<ref name=":53" /> While a slight majority of American teenagers attending public schools wore religious symbols and attire, they were much less likely to pray before lunch or a sport event, invite their peers to join a religious club, and to read religious texts outside of class.<ref name="Pew-2019a">{{Cite news |last= |first= |date=October 3, 2019 |title=For a Lot of American Teens, Religion Is a Regular Part of the Public School Day |url=https://www.pewforum.org/2019/10/03/for-a-lot-of-american-teens-religion-is-a-regular-part-of-the-public-school-day/ |access-date=December 1, 2019 |work=Pew Research Center |department=Religion}}</ref> Girls were more likely to discuss religion with their friends than boys.<ref name="Pew-2019a" />

Members of Generation Z were more likely to start questioning their parents' religions before the age of 18 than previous cohorts and those who have left typically did not return.<ref name=":59" /> Much of the decline of religion in the United States is due to people born after 1990 leaving their families' faiths.<ref>{{Cite news |last=King |first=Jordan |date=November 14, 2025 |title=US Decline In Religion Among Biggest In World |url=https://www.newsweek.com/us-decline-in-religion-among-biggest-in-world-11047526 |access-date=November 14, 2025 |work=Newsweek}}</ref> Young adults born in the 2000s rarely become Christian after being raised in a non-Christian household.<ref name=":61">{{Cite news |last=Smith |first=Gregory A. |date=December 8, 2025 |title=Religion Holds Steady in America |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/12/08/religion-holds-steady-in-america/ |access-date=December 10, 2025 |work=Pew Research Center}}</ref> A majority of Generation Z disagreed that it was necessary to raise children in a religious household,<ref name=":59">{{Cite web |last=Cox |first=Daniel A. |date=March 24, 2022 |title=Generation Z and the Future of Faith in America |url=https://www.americansurveycenter.org/research/generation-z-future-of-faith/ |access-date=March 27, 2023 |website=American Enterprise Institute}}</ref> and only a minority deemed religion to be an important part of their lives.<ref name="Zitner-2023">{{Cite news |last=Zitner |first=Aaron |date=March 27, 2023 |title=Americans Pull Back From Values That Once Defined U.S., WSJ-NORC Poll Finds |work=The Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.wsj.com/amp/articles/americans-pull-back-from-values-that-once-defined-u-s-wsj-norc-poll-finds-df8534cd |access-date=March 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/4aheK |archive-date=March 28, 2023}}</ref> On the other hand, the Pew Research Center found the gap in spirituality among the old and the young to be more modest.<ref name=":53" />

In a 2016 poll, [[Barna Group|Barna]] found that Millennials and Generation Z were equally likely to require factual evidence before believing in something and to consider the Bible to be at odds with science.<ref name="Barna.com-2018">{{cite web|last=|first=|date=January 24, 2018|title=Atheism Doubles Among Generation Z|url=https://www.barna.com/research/atheism-doubles-among-generation-z/|access-date=October 31, 2019|website=Barna.com|publisher=Barna Group}}</ref> The same Barna survey revealed that the percentage of [[Atheism in the United States|atheists]] and agnostics was 21% among Generation Z, higher than all previous cohorts.<ref name="Barna.com-2018" /> Moreover, whereas in the past, women were broadly more religious than men, during the 2020s, young women secularizing faster than young men,<ref name=":15">{{Cite news |last=Ramirez |first=Marc |date=August 13, 2024 |title=Americans are becoming less religious. None more than this group |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2024/08/13/gen-z-women-less-religious/74673083007/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240813143001/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2024/08/13/gen-z-women-less-religious/74673083007/ |archive-date=August 13, 2024 |access-date=October 11, 2024 |work=USA Today |department=Nation}}</ref><ref name=":25">{{Cite news |last=Graham |first=Ruth |date=September 23, 2024 |title=In a First Among Christians, Young Men Are More Religious Than Young Women |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/23/us/young-men-religion-gen-z.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20241006033833/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/23/us/young-men-religion-gen-z.html |archive-date=October 6, 2024 |access-date=October 14, 2024 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name=":40">{{Cite news |last=Contreras |first=Russell |date=September 28, 2024 |title=Young women grow less religious than young men |url=https://www.axios.com/2024/09/28/religion-poll-gen-z-men-women-gap |access-date=October 31, 2024 |work=Axios}}</ref> and have become just about as religious as men.<ref name=":61" /> Youths who still hold private religious beliefs are also less likely to go to church.<ref name=":25" /> When asked what their biggest barriers to faith were, [[Irreligion in the United States|irreligious]] members of Generation Z pointed to what they perceived as internal contradictions of the religion and its believers.<ref name="Barna.com-2018" /> Many also took issue with religious leaders' positions on certain social and political topics, such as abortion, homosexuality, and sex-abuse scandals of the Church.<ref name=":15" /><ref name=":40" /> Young women in particular disapproved of the Church's emphasis on traditional gender roles, especially the [[Patriarchy|subservience of women before men]], and the [[Purity culture|culture of purity]], such as the insistence that women must dress "modestly" because they were responsible for the thoughts of men. Living in the Age of Information, they found it easy to be disillusioned by religious teachings and to deconvert themselves.<ref name=":15" /> Women having access to higher education, having careers, and deprioritizing matrimony and reproduction were also contributing factors.<ref name=":15" />

== Risky behaviors ==

=== General trends ===
Research from the [[Annie E. Casey Foundation]] conducted in 2016 found Generation Z youth had lower teen pregnancy rates, less substance abuse, and higher on-time high school graduation rates compared with Millennials. The researchers compared teens from 2008 and 2014 and found a 40% drop in teen pregnancy, a 38% drop in drug and alcohol abuse, and a 28% drop in the percentage of teens who did not graduate on time from high school.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/generation-z-breaks-records-in-education-and-health-despite-growing-economic-instability-of-their-families-300287848.html|title=Generation Z Breaks Records in Education and Health Despite Growing Economic Instability of Their Families|date=21 June 2016|access-date=22 June 2016|publisher=PR Newswire}}</ref><ref name="Blad-2016">{{cite news|url=http://blogs.edweek.org/edweek/rulesforengagement/2016/06/teenagers_health_educational_outcomes_improving_report_finds.html|title=Teenagers' Health, Educational Outcomes Improving, Report Finds|last1=Blad|first1=Evie|date=21 June 2016|access-date=22 June 2016|publisher=Education Week}}</ref> Three-quarters of American twelfth-graders believed their peers disapproved of binge drinking.<ref name="Schepis-2020">{{Cite news|last=Schepis|first=Ty|date=November 19, 2020|title=College-age kids and teens are drinking less alcohol – marijuana is a different story|work=The Conversation|url=https://theconversation.com/college-age-kids-and-teens-are-drinking-less-alcohol-marijuana-is-a-different-story-149895|access-date=November 21, 2020}}</ref> Members of Generation Z tend to be more worried about mental health issues and getting good grades than unplanned pregnancies or binge drinking.<ref name="The Economist-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2019/02/27/generation-z-is-stressed-depressed-and-exam-obsessed|title=Generation Z is stressed, depressed and exam-obsessed|date=2019-02-27|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=2019-03-28|issn=0013-0613}}</ref>

=== Cigarette-smoking and substance abuse ===
[[File:High School Smoking 2.png|center]]
Although the number of American teenagers who smoked cigarettes was steadily falling during the 2010s, the prevalence of [[electronic cigarette]] use was rising. As of 2019, there is no evidence linking the availability of electronic cigarettes to a decline in traditional smoking among youths. Public opinion has turned against electronic cigarettes and various state and local governments are seeking to restrict use.<ref name="Perrone-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://apnews.com/d64be73398c443089b0421e8f29da419|title=Vape debate: Are e-cigarettes wiping out teen smoking?|last=Perrone|first=Matthew|date=November 21, 2019|work=Associated Press|access-date=December 2, 2019}}</ref> By the mid-2020s, tobacco product use of all types among teenagers was on the decline, a trend largely driven by falling e-cigarette demand.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kekatos |first=Mary |date=October 17, 2024 |title=Tobacco product use among middle, high school students hits 25-year low: Report |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/tobacco-product-middle-high-school-students-hits-25/story?id=114887327 |access-date=October 18, 2024 |work=ABC News}}</ref>

Bloomberg reported in 2019 that members of Generation Z were twice as likely as an average American to consume [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]]. About 1% of the number of legal marijuana consumers came this demographic cohort, and that number tripled in 2019. Generation Z is the first to be born into a time when the [[Decriminalization of non-medical cannabis in the United States|legalization of marijuana]] at the federal level is being seriously considered.<ref name="Ayesh-2019">{{Cite news|url=https://www.axios.com/gen-z-buys-more-marijuana-anyone-else-fb60a20f-df38-41c0-bc37-2b27557dfe38.html|title=Survey: Gen Z twice as likely to use marijuana than national average|last=Ayesh|first=Rashaan|date=April 20, 2019|work=Axios|access-date=September 5, 2019|archive-date=April 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190421202953/https://www.axios.com/gen-z-buys-more-marijuana-anyone-else-fb60a20f-df38-41c0-bc37-2b27557dfe38.html}}</ref> As of 2019, cannabis is legal in 33 U.S. states as well as in Canada and Uruguay.<ref name="Sohn-2019">{{Cite journal|last=Sohn|first=Emily|date=August 28, 2019|title=Weighing the dangers of cannabis|journal=Nature|volume=572|issue=7771|pages=S16–S18|doi=10.1038/d41586-019-02530-7|pmid=31462789|bibcode=2019Natur.572S..16S|s2cid=201665162|doi-access=free}}</ref> Even though Generation Z may not think of cannabis as anything more than a controversial issue, there is mounting concern on its effects on human health.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/julianvigo/2019/08/31/generation-z-and-new-technologys-effect-on-culture/#6e7b204d5c2a|title=Generation Z And New Technology's Effect On Culture|last=Vigo|first=Julian|date=August 31, 2019|work=Forbes|access-date=September 5, 2019}}</ref> A survey of literature reveals that marijuana usage is linked to, among other things, impaired driving, higher risks of stroke, testicular cancer, memory loss, and certain mental illnesses, such as [[psychosis]]. Compared to those who do not use cannabis or those who start after they reach 16 years, people who start before that age suffer from reduced cognitive functioning and higher levels of impulsivity.<ref name="Sohn-2019" /> About one in ten marijuana users developed a [[substance use disorder]], and those who use it before the age of 18 are more likely to suffer from it.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/marijuana/illinois/ct-marijuana-illinois-health-effects-20191224-j2qafgizjbe5vibxrajgw7c6kq-story.html|title=Thinking of buying pot in Illinois on Jan. 1? Here's how experts say it could affect your health — for better and for worse|last=McCoppin|first=Robert|date=December 24, 2019|work=Chicago Tribune|access-date=December 24, 2019}}</ref> Marijuana use in the United States is three times above the global average, but in line with other Western democracies. Forty-four percent of American high-school seniors have tried the drug at least once, and the typical age of first-use is 16, similar to the typical age of first-use for alcohol but lower than the first-use age for other illicit drugs.<ref name="CaulkinsHawken2012">{{cite book |last1=Caulkins |first1=Jonathan P. |url=https://archive.org/details/marijuanalegaliz0000unse/page/16 |title=Marijuana Legalization: What Everyone Needs to Know |last2=Hawken |first2=Angela |last3=Kilmer |first3=Beau |last4=Kleiman |first4=Mark A.R. |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-19-991373-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/marijuanalegaliz0000unse/page/16 16] |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>

=== Early sexual intercourse and adolescent pregnancy ===
[[File:US teen birth rate by state.svg |thumb | Teen birth rate by state in 2015]]
[[File:1991- Birth rate for teenagers (US).svg |thumb |Teen birth rates have declined over the past few decades.<ref name=CDC_20260409>Figure 2 of: {{cite web |last1=Hamilton |first1=Brady E. |last2=Osterman |first2=Michelle J.K. |last3=Gregory |first3=Elizabeth C.W. |title=Vital Statistics Rapid Release / Report Number 43 |url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/vsrr/vsrr043.pdf |publisher=U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / National Vital Statistics System |page=3 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260410011958/https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/vsrr/vsrr043.pdf |archive-date=10 April 2026 |date=9 April 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

{{See also|Teenage pregnancy in the United States}}
Historically, the birth rate of teenagers peaked in the late 1950s and early 1960s. However, at that time, most teenage parents were married.<ref name="Patten-2016">{{Cite web|last1=Patten|first1=Eileen|last2=Livingston|first2=Gretchen|date=April 29, 2016|title=Why is the teen birth rate falling?|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2016/04/29/why-is-the-teen-birth-rate-falling/|access-date=July 2, 2019|website=Pew Research Center}}</ref> In the early twenty-first century, nine in ten births to the age group 15-19 are to unmarried mothers.<ref name="Patten-2016" />

Social norms have changed; it is now not unusual for teenagers to delay or avoid sexual intercourse altogether. Younger teenagers are more likely to practice abstinence than their older counterparts.<ref name="Cha-2016" /> A report published by the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|Center for Disease Control and Prevention]] (CDC) in early 2018 found the number of high school students who have had sex fell from 47% in 2005 down to 41% in 2015, with the most dramatic drop taking place between 2013 and 2015.<ref name="Politico-chill">{{Cite journal|last=|first=|date=February 8, 2018|title=Too Much Netflix, Not Enough Chill: Why Young Americans Are Having Less Sex|url=https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2018/02/08/why-young-americans-having-less-sex-216953/|journal=Politico Magazine|volume=|pages=|via=}}</ref> On top of that, among never-married teens who have had sex, overwhelming majorities reported they used contraception the first time they did it.<ref name="Patten-2016" /> There are a few reasons for this. First, Millennials and Generation Z are more focused on the consequences of sex than their predecessors were. Second, there has been growing concern over unwanted sexual advances, especially in the wake of the Me-too movement. Writing for ''The Spectator'', [[Douglas Murray (author)|Douglas Murray]] dubbed this the "sexual counter-revolution."<ref group="note">As opposed to the Sexual Revolution of the 1960s, which saw the liberalization of attitudes towards sex.</ref> Third, as a consequence of the precarious contemporary economy, young adults today are more likely to be living with their parents rather than on their own, with a romantic partner, or a spouse.<ref name="Politico-chill" />

A 2016 analysis by the CDC discovered that teenage birthrates nosedived between 1991, when they reached a crisis point, and 2014, when they dropped by 60%, a record low. The collapse of birthrates among blacks and (non-white) Hispanics, down 50%, was largely responsible for this development. However, their birthrates remained, on average, twice as high as those of their white counterparts.<ref name="Cha-2016" /> The birth rates of teenage Asians and Pacific Islanders were even lower, about half that of whites.<ref name="Patten-2016" /> In a 2014 paper, economists [[Melissa Kearney|Melissa S. Kearney]] and Phillip B. Levine howed that popular TV programs depicting the reality of teenage parenthood, such as MTV's ''[[16 and Pregnant]]'' and its ''[[Teen Mom]]'' sequels, have played a significant role in the reduction of teenage childbearing.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Kearney|first1=Melissa|last2=Levine|first2=Phillip|date=January 15, 2014|title=Media Influences on Social Outcomes: The Impact of MTV's "16 and Pregnant" on Teen Childbearing|url=https://www.brookings.edu/research/media-influences-on-social-outcomes-the-impact-of-mtvs-16-and-pregnant-on-teen-childbearing/|access-date=July 2, 2019|website=The Brookings Institution}}</ref> Researchers from the [[Guttmacher Institute]] showed that the fall in teenage birthrates is likely not due to terminated pregnancies. The number of abortions remained the same or decreased in all U.S. states except for Vermont.<ref name="Cha-2016" /><ref group="note">According to [https://www.guttmacher.org/fact-sheet/induced-abortion-worldwide this 2018 report] from the Guttmacher Institute, Western Europe, North America, and Northern Europe have the lowest abortions rates globally, at 16, 17, and 18 per a thousand women of reproductive age, respectively.</ref> This contradicts the historically negative correlation between birthrates and abortions. Modern youths also have better access to contraception than did their predecessors when they were at the same age.<ref name="Cha-2016" /> A CDC analysis found that the rates of teens using a long-acting and reversible method of contraception, such as an intrauterine device ([[Intrauterine device|IUD]]), jumped from 0.4% in 2005 to 7.1% in 2013.<ref name="Patten-2016" /> The teen birthrate continues to fall in the late 2010s, down to 17.4 births per 1000 in 2018.<ref name="Edwards-2019">{{Cite news |last=Edwards |first=Erika |date=November 27, 2019 |title=U.S. birth rate falls for 4th year in a row |work=NBC News |department=Health News |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/u-s-birth-rate-falls-4th-year-row-n1091446 |access-date=January 1, 2020}}</ref> In 2022, it fell to 13.5, the lowest on record.<ref name="Kekatos-2023">{{Cite news |last=Kekatos |first=Mary |date=June 1, 2023 |title=Teenage birth rates in the US reached historic lows in 2022, CDC report finds |work=ABC News |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/teenage-birth-rates-us-reached-historic-lows-2022/story?id=99720479 |access-date=December 7, 2023}}</ref>

==Social trends==

=== Upbringing ===
{{multiple image
| direction         = vertical
| align             = right
| width             = 300
| footer            = 
| image1            = American Household Composition Past and Present.png
| caption1          = By the time of Generation Z, the [[nuclear family]] had ceased to be the norm.
| image2            = Elementary School Orchestra.jpg
| caption2          = An elementary school orchestra (2009). Contemporary American parents tend to invest more in their children's cultural capital.
| width1            = 
| perrow            = 1 / 2 / 1
}}

Between the 1960s and the 2010s, the percentage of children living with their married parents in their first marriage declined from approximately three quarters to just under half. At the same time, the share of children raised by single parents rose sharply.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Livingston|first=Gretchen|date=December 22, 2014|title=Fewer than half of U.S. kids today live in a 'traditional' family|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2014/12/22/less-than-half-of-u-s-kids-today-live-in-a-traditional-family/|access-date=November 15, 2020|website=Pew Research Center}}</ref> During the 2000s and 2010s, the number of American children raised by their grandparents or other family members rather than their parents also grew.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cancino |first=Alejandra |date=February 16, 2016 |title=More grandparents raising their grandchildren |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/more-grandparents-raising-their-grandchildren |access-date=February 25, 2020 |work=PBS Newshour |department=Nation}}</ref>

American parents of the early twenty-first century usually do not insist that their children share the same political or religious beliefs, to follow the same traditions, or to get married and have children. Rather, they emphasize ethical behavior, tolerance, generosity, and financial independence.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Minkin |first1=Rachel |last2=Horowitz |first2=Juliana Menasce |date=January 24, 2023 |title=Parenting in America Today |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2023/01/24/parenting-in-america-today/ |access-date=January 27, 2023 |work=Pew Research Center}}</ref>

Parents from wealthier backgrounds are less likely to have children out of wedlock and more likely to stay married, with desirable outcomes for their children, including better social and cognitive development and educational attainment. By contrast, children born into the middle class or the lower class are less likely to have married parents than before.<ref name="Reeves-2020">{{Cite web |last1=Reeves |first1=Richard V. |last2=Pulliam |first2=Christopher |date=March 11, 2020 |title=Middle class marriage is declining, and likely deepening inequality |url=https://www.brookings.edu/research/middle-class-marriage-is-declining-and-likely-deepening-inequality/ |access-date=January 26, 2023 |website=Brookings Institution}}</ref> They also tend to have younger parents who [[Unintended pregnancy|did not intend to have them]] and more siblings.<ref name="Bui-2018">{{Cite news |last1=Bui |first1=Quoctrung |last2=Miller |first2=Claire Cain |date=August 4, 2018 |title=The Age That Women Have Babies: How a Gap Divides America |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/08/04/upshot/up-birth-age-gap.html |access-date=April 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20210620122837/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/08/04/upshot/up-birth-age-gap.html |archive-date=June 20, 2021}}</ref> Upper middle-class and wealthy American couples living in the cities tend to have fewer children and to invest heavily in their children in the form of [[breastfeeding]] for at least a year, giving them premium healthcare plans, sending them to private schools, and letting them eat [[organic food]]s.<ref name=":36" /><ref name=":37" /><ref name=":38" /> Among those who send their children to public schools, they favor policies that ensure the high quality of such schools with exclusionary admissions and [[Zoning in the United States|zoning]] ordinances.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sreenivasan |first=Hari |date=August 5, 2017 |title=How the upper middle class keeps everyone else out |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/upper-middle-class-keeps-everyone-else |access-date=October 31, 2024 |work=PBS News Hour}}</ref> Said parents also hire nannies and housekeepers to reduce the time they spend doing house chores so that they can more time on culturally and educationally [[Extracurricular activity|enriching activities]] with their children.<ref name=":36">{{Cite news|last=Kopf|first=Dan|date=June 11, 2017|title=The new, nearly invisible class markers that separate the American elite from everyone else|work=Quartz|url=https://qz.com/999078/the-new-conspicuous-consumption-is-a-lacrosse-playing-child-and-an-npr-tote-bag/|access-date=September 11, 2021|archive-url=https://archive.today/20210612143556/https://qz.com/999078/the-new-conspicuous-consumption-is-a-lacrosse-playing-child-and-an-npr-tote-bag/|archive-date=June 12, 2021}}</ref><ref name=":37">{{Cite news|date=August 5, 2017|title=Modern American elites have come to favour inconspicuous consumption|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/books-and-arts/2017/08/05/modern-american-elites-have-come-to-favour-inconspicuous-consumption|access-date=September 11, 2021|archive-url=https://archive.today/20190509002300/https://www.economist.com/books-and-arts/2017/08/05/modern-american-elites-have-come-to-favour-inconspicuous-consumption|archive-date=May 9, 2019}}</ref><ref name=":38">{{Cite news |last=Currid-Halkett |first=Elizabeth |author-link=Elizabeth Currid-Halkett |date=June 14, 2017 |title=The new, subtle ways the rich signal their wealth |work=BBC Future |url=https://www.bbc.com/worklife/article/20170614-the-new-subtle-ways-the-rich-signal-their-wealth |access-date=September 11, 2021}}</ref> In fact, the amount of time parents spend with their children has gone up since the mid-1960s, especially among educated couples.<ref>{{Cite news|date=November 27, 2017|title=Parents now spend twice as much time with their children as 50 years ago|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2017/11/27/parents-now-spend-twice-as-much-time-with-their-children-as-50-years-ago|access-date=January 17, 2022|archive-url=https://archive.today/20191224170541/https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2017/11/27/parents-now-spend-twice-as-much-time-with-their-children-as-50-years-ago|archive-date=December 24, 2019}}</ref> An early start to the accumulation of [[cultural capital]] helps children stand out from the competition as they mature, making them more likely to be admitted to prestigious universities.<ref name="Westover-2019">{{Cite news |last=Westover |first=Tara |date=September 12, 2019 |title=Is College Merely Helping Those Who Need Help Least? |work=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/11/books/review/the-years-that-matter-most-paul-tough.html |access-date=August 22, 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20190917132003/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/11/books/review/the-years-that-matter-most-paul-tough.html |archive-date=September 17, 2019}}</ref>

On the other hand, Generation Z typically grows up with less independence than the Baby Boomers or Generation X.<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> This constant supervision of children by their parents—protective or "[[helicopter parent]]ing"—is partly due to concerns over public safety or legal requirements<ref name=":24">{{Cite news |last1=Brangham |first1=William |last2=Kane |first2=Jason |date=December 17, 2018 |title=Why helicopter parenting may jeopardize kids' health |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/why-helicopter-parenting-may-jeopardize-kids-health |access-date=October 14, 2024 |work=PBS News Hour}}</ref> and partly due to the fact that many educators and parents view [[Play (activity)|play]] as outdated and irrelevant.<ref name="Klass-2018" /> As a result, a portion of this cohort spends much of their leisure in doors rather than outside, with little to no adult supervision.<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> In reality, the United States has become a safer place for children, who are much less likely to be abducted or otherwise harmed by an adult than ever before.<ref name=":24" /> In 2018, the [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] released a statement emphasizing the importance of unstructured time spent by children pointing to the benefits for children's social, cognitive, and language skills development.<ref name="Klass-2018" /> Play can also help children handle stress, including [[Stress in early childhood|toxic stress]],<ref name="Klass-2018">{{Cite news |last=Klass |first=Perri |date=August 20, 2018 |title=Let Kids Play - Doctors should prescribe playtime for young children, the American Academy of Pediatrics says |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/20/well/family/let-kids-play.html |access-date=August 4, 2019 |work=The New York Times |department=The Checkup}}</ref> and reduce their chances of being obese or depressed.<ref name=":24" />

=== Time-spending habits and leisure ===
[[File:Kids Camp 2015 Day 3 (18936933418).jpg|thumb|Two children playing chess at a summer camp (2015)]]
According to the Pew Research Center, American teenagers of the 2010s on average spent more time doing homework and sleeping compared to their counterparts from the previous decade.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Livingston |first=Gretchen |date=2019-02-20 |title=The way U.S. teens spend their time is changing, but differences between boys and girls persist |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/02/20/the-way-u-s-teens-spend-their-time-is-changing-but-differences-between-boys-and-girls-persist/ |access-date=2026-07-23 |website=Pew Research Center |language=en-US}}</ref> (However, other surveys suggest teens get fewer hours of sleep each day.) They also spent less time at paid jobs and on socializing. Meanwhile, the amount of time spent on sports, clothes shopping, and volitional reading have not changed.<ref name="Livingston-2019">{{Cite web|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2019/02/20/the-way-u-s-teens-spend-their-time-is-changing-but-differences-between-boys-and-girls-persist/|title=The way U.S. teens spend their time is changing, but differences between boys and girls persist|last=Livingston|first=Gretchen|date=February 20, 2019|website=Pew Research Center|access-date=June 16, 2019}}</ref> But there were differences in how teenage boys and girls spent their free time. Boys generally spent more time on leisure activities, such as playing sports and on their electronic devices, whereas girls spent more time on homework, housework, and activities related to appearance. Girls also spent more time on volunteering and on unpaid care work than boys. Pluralities of both sexes said they felt pressured to look good, especially girls.<ref name="Livingston-2019" /> In general, Generation Z is less likely to engage in "fringe" behavior.<ref name="HuffPo-2017" />

Generation Z tends to be lonelier than ever before.<ref name="The Economist-2019" /> A study of social interaction among American teenagers found that the amount of time young people spent with their friends had been trending downwards since the 1970s but has fallen sharply after 2010. Teenagers of the 2010s attended parties less often compared to their counterparts in the 1980s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Twenge |first=Jean |date=March 20, 2019 |title=Teens have less face time with their friends – and are lonelier than ever |url=http://theconversation.com/teens-have-less-face-time-with-their-friends-and-are-lonelier-than-ever-113240 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211212145657/https://theconversation.com/teens-have-less-face-time-with-their-friends-and-are-lonelier-than-ever-113240 |archive-date=December 12, 2021 |access-date=December 12, 2021 |website=The Conversation |language=en}}</ref> Despite the technological proficiency they possess, 72% generally prefer person-to-person contact as opposed to online interaction.<ref name="Desjardins-2019" /><ref name="Levit-2015">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/03/29/jobs/make-way-for-generation-z.html|title=Make Way for Generation Z|last=Levit|first=Alexandra|date=28 March 2015|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=22 December 2015|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The desire for in-person interactions has fueled the revival of [[board game]]s such as [[backgammon]], [[chess]], and [[mahjong]] among Millennials and Generation Z.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Holtermann |first1=Callie |last2=Dickie |first2=Graham |date=December 17, 2024 |title=The Extremely Offline Joy of the Board Game Club |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/17/style/board-games-club.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250227031738/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/17/style/board-games-club.html |archive-date=February 27, 2025 |access-date=March 12, 2025 |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

=== Romance, marriage, and family ===
{{See also|Going steady}}
A press release by the online dating app [[Tinder (app)|Tinder]] showed that the age group 18 to 24 became the majority of users on their platform in 2019. The company boasted 7.86 million users in the United States that year.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Moore |first=Courtney |date=January 1, 2020 |title=Tinder year ender: How Gen Z changed dating in 2019 |url=https://www.foxbusiness.com/technology/tinder-year-ender-how-gen-z-changed-dating-in-2019 |access-date=January 3, 2020 |work=Fox Business |department=Tech}}</ref> Nevertheless, even though smartphone applications such as Tinder allow for easy [[Hookup culture|hook-ups]] and [[one-night stand]]s, Millennials and Generation Z are quite serious and cautious when it comes to long-term romantic relationships.<ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last=Bote |first=Joshua |date=July 29, 2019 |title=Millennial and Gen Z singles have enough casual sex. But they want love, survey says |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2019/07/29/match-singles-survey-millennials-gen-z-want-love-have-sex/1861101001/ |access-date=August 2, 2019 |work=USA Today}}</ref> Unlike generations past, who married earlier and after shorter periods of courtship, Generation Z generally prefers to take things slowly.<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> Generation Z, especially women, is also more likely to have been friends with a romantic partner before dating. Daniel Cox of [[FiveThirtyEight|Five Thirty Eight]] explains, "This suggests a significant push back [among young Americans] against [[online dating]] as a way to meet partners."<ref name=":13">{{Cite news |last=Thomson-DeVeaux |first=Amelia |date=February 14, 2023 |title=Americans Are Increasingly Single And OK With It |url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/more-americans-are-choosing-to-stay-single/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230215014342/https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/more-americans-are-choosing-to-stay-single/ |archive-date=February 15, 2023 |access-date=September 29, 2024 |work=Five Thirty Eight}}</ref> Most members of this cohort prefer monogamy.<ref name=":47">{{Cite news |last=Blake |first=Suzanne |date=April 14, 2025 |title=Gen Z Is More Like Boomers Than We Think: Study |url=https://www.newsweek.com/gen-z-more-like-boomers-we-think-study-2059662 |access-date=May 17, 2025 |work=Newsweek}}</ref> However, a significant number is [[Singleton (lifestyle)|choosing to remain single]], because they do not want to be in a relationship, are facing trouble meeting the right people, or have other priorities at present, such as (higher) education or careers.<ref name=":13" /><ref name="Twenge-2023a" /> Data from the 2019 General Social Survey revealed that 51% of Americans aged 18 to 24 had no steady partner, higher than other cohorts. Moreover, this number has grown in recent years.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Bonos|first1=Lisa|last2=Guskin|first2=Emily|date=March 21, 2019|title=It's not just you: New data shows more than half of young people in America don't have a romantic partner|newspaper=The Washington Post|department=Relationships|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2019/03/21/its-not-just-you-new-data-shows-more-than-half-young-people-america-dont-have-romantic-partner/|access-date=September 19, 2021|archive-url=https://archive.today/20191217211620/https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2019/03/21/its-not-just-you-new-data-shows-more-than-half-young-people-america-dont-have-romantic-partner/|archive-date=December 17, 2019}}</ref> Men below the age of 30 are much more likely to be single than women in the same age group.<ref name=":41" />

Although a majority of Millennials and Generation Z would like to get married one day, two fifths [[Criticism of marriage|deem marriage to be an outdated institution]] and an overwhelming majority think it is unnecessary for a fulfilling or happy life.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nazzaro |first=Miranda |date=July 20, 2023 |title=2 in 5 young adults surveyed say marriage an outdated tradition |url=https://thehill.com/changing-america/respect/equality/4107946-2-in-5-young-adults-surveyed-say-marriage-an-outdated-tradition/ |access-date=September 29, 2024 |work=The Hill}}</ref> Moreover, they generally prefer an equitable partnership to a traditional patriarchal arrangement.<ref name=":47" /> Surveys have also documented a marked decline in the desire for children.<ref name="Twenge-2023a" /><ref name="Leanne"/> Close to a quarter of Millennials and Generation Z say [[Voluntary childlessness|they do not want children]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dickler |first=Jessica |date=September 24, 2024 |title='Childless cat lady' is a more common lifestyle choice.
